He commanded His Prophet (ﷺ) that he should say this speech and warn by the Qur'an every one it reaches, and He did not restrict it to humans or jinn among those who are responsible; and there is no disagreement that the jinn are responsible. End of quote. What has been mentioned of the verses and others will come, which is fitting as evidence for the sending to the angels, peace be upon them. The meaning is: whoever believes this Qur'an has prospered, and whoever denies it, let him produce a surah like it. Then his inability is itself a witness against himself of falsehood, while it is Allah's testimony to my truthfulness. Because Allah is the Witness, the testimony was not annulled by the death of the Prophet (ﷺ); rather it continues through the passing days and years, because the Witness endures and is exalted above any defect of deficiency or the marks of created things. To this the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying alludes: "There was no prophet among the prophets except that he was given signs such that people believed on account of them; but what I was given is a revelation that Allah revealed to me, so I hope to be the most numerous of them in following on the Day of Resurrection." Related by the two Shaykhs (al-Bukhari and Muslim), from Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him. Perhaps the limitation to warning, along with what has preceded, indicates that most of creation is lost. It has been mentioned, regarding the revelation of this verse, that the people of Makkah came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: "Has Allah not found a messenger other than you? We see no one believing what you say. We asked the Jews and Christians about you, and they claimed that there is no mention of you with them. So show us someone who testifies that you are the Messenger of Allah as you claim." So Allah revealed it.

When there remained no pretext for the stubborn, He brought the conclusion of that and the pivot of its circle, which is the necessity of tawhid (monotheism), upon which the message was made a ladder to ascend; when it is established in a heart, its lights overflow according to its steadfastness, to the point that they may fill the worlds and rise above Kaywan (Saturn). He brought it as a question in the manner of denial and wonder, exalting His affair, magnifying His station, and alerting them to keep far from associating partners. So He said: ﴿Do you truly testify that with Allah there are other gods?﴾, that is, He who has gathered all greatness. ﴿Gods﴾... Since they, because of their great obstinacy, might apply the name "god" to His names—glorified is He—as they said when they heard him (ﷺ) say "O Allah, O Merciful" (as will come, Allah willing, at the end of al-Hijr and at the end of Subhan), He stated the intended meaning in a way that admits no dispute, saying: ﴿another﴾. And since it was as if it were said: "They indeed say that, so what is to be said to them?" He said: ﴿Say: I do not testify﴾, that is, with you to anything you say, because it is falsehood, and if it were true I would have testified to it.

Since this was not decisive in cutting off their hope in it, He uprooted it from its origin and entirety by saying: ﴿Say: He is only one God﴾, that is, the Deity, ﴿one God﴾, and He is Allah, who (p-45) cannot be overcome by anything and overcomes everything, because He is One with no equal. For you were unable to bring a surah like His speech, and you are the most eloquent of people.

Since the meaning of this is disavowal of their warning, He stated it in His words, emphasized in a nominal sentence: ﴿And indeed I am free of what you associate﴾, that is, now and in the future, to remove any hope on their part that agreement might exist between him and them by his taking rivals or any of them as a friend. Thus tawhid was established by this verse with the greatest ways of exposition and the most eloquent forms of emphasis. The Prophet (ﷺ) indeed complied with the command to warn whoever the Qur'an could reach. When he was relieved from fighting the Quraysh and many of the Arabs around him in the year of al-Hudaybiyah, which was the sixth year after the Hijrah, and Allah informed him that this was a manifest victory, he sent to those kings of the regions in that year and afterward. Most of them, at his return from that 'umrah, he called to gardens and rivers in the abode of permanence, and warned them of the abode of ruin. The historians said: "After his return from the 'Umrah of al-Hudaybiyah, from which he had been prevented, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) went out to his companions—may Allah be pleased with them all—and said: 'O people! Allah has sent me as a mercy and for all people, and I want to send some of you to the kings of the non-Arabs.'" Ibn 'Abd al-Hakam said in Futuh Misr, from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Abd al-Qadir: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) stood one day on the pulpit, praised Allah, extolled Him, and recited the tashahhud (p-46), then said: 'Now then, I want to send some of you to the kings of the non-Arabs, so convey from me, may Allah have mercy on you, and do not differ over me as the disciples differed.'"

Ibn 'Abd al-Hakam also said: "The Children of Israel differed over 'Isa ibn Maryam, peace be upon them both. The emigrants said: 'O Messenger of Allah! By Allah, we will never differ over you in anything ever; so command us and send us.' They asked him: 'How did the disciples differ over 'Isa, peace be upon him?' He said: 'He called them to what—' and in another narration: 'to the like of what I have called you to.'" Ibn 'Abd al-Hakam also said: Allah, blessed and exalted, revealed to 'Isa, peace be upon him, that he should send to the holy land (Maqdis al-Ard). So the disciples were sent: those whom he sent on a near mission were content and submitted, while those whom he sent on a distant mission disliked its direction and was reluctant. Ibn 'Abd al-Hakam said: He said, "I do not know how to speak the language of those to whom you send me." So 'Isa, peace be upon him, complained of this to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and every man (Ibn 'Abd al-Hakam said) ... Allah revealed to him: "I will suffice you," so the reluctant ones awoke, and each one of them was speaking the language of the nation to which he was sent. 'Isa, peace be upon him, said: "This is a matter that Allah has decreed, so proceed with it." Shaykh Majd al-Din al-Fayruzabadi said in al-Qamus: The place where 'Isa, peace be upon him, gathered the disciples and dispatched them to the regions is a village in the district of Tiberias called al-Kursi. Ibn Ishaq said: Yazid ibn Abi Habib al-Misri (p-47) related to me that he found a book in which was mentioned those whom the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent to the lands and to the kings of the Arabs and the non-Arabs, and what he said to his companions when he sent them. He sent it to Muhammad ibn Shihab al-Zuhri, who recognized it, and he mentioned something like what preceded, until he said: Ibn Ishaq said: Among those sent by 'Isa ibn Maryam (ﷺ) from the disciples and the followers who were after them in the earth were Butrus (Peter) the disciple, with Bulus (Paul)—who was among the followers, not among the disciples—to Rome; Andrayas and Mantha to the land whose people eat people; Tawmas to the land of Babylon in the land of the East; Qaybalis to Carthage, which is Ifriqiyya; Yahnas to Ansus, the village of the Companions of the Cave (al-Fityah); Ya'qubus to Urashlim, which is Aelia, the village of Bayt al-Maqdis; Ibn Thalma to the Arabs, which is the land of the Hijaz; Sayman to the land of the Berbers; and Yahuda, who was not among the disciples, was put in place of Yudas. End of quote. Thus I saw in an authoritative collated copy of the Tahdhib al-Sirah of Ibn Hisham; and likewise in its abridgement by the Imam Jamal al-Din Muhammad ibn al-Mukarram al-Ansari, the number of his messengers and their names, and at its end the phrase "in place of Yudas," though no mention of Yudas had preceded. What I have verified myself from the Gospels in the hands of the Christians is other than this, and it is perhaps more accurate. I have gathered what is scattered of their wording. In the Gospel of Matthew, its text is: and most of the context concerning him: He (that is, 'Isa, peace be upon him) called his twelve disciples and gave them authority over all the unclean spirits, to cast them out and to heal every disease. In the Gospel of Mark: He went up the mountain and called those whom he loved, and they came to him, and he chose twelve to be with him and to send them forth to preach, and gave them authority to heal diseases and cast out demons. In the Gospel of Luke: In those days he went out to the mountain to pray, and he was persevering in the prayer of God; when day came he called his disciples and chose from them twelve. And he said in another place: He called the twelve apostles and gave them power and authority over all demons and to heal the sick, and sent them to preach the kingdom of God and to heal the sick;

This is the list of the twelve apostles: Simon, called Peter, whose father is named in one place in the Gospel (Injil) of Matthew as "son of Jonah"; his brother Andrew; James son of Zebedee; his brother John; (p-49) and he says in the Gospel of Mark that he named the two of them "Boanerges," meaning "sons of thunder." Also Philip and Bartholomew; Thomas and Matthew the tax collector; James son of Alphaeus; and Lebbaeus, who is called Thaddaeus. In the Gospel of Mark he puts Thaddaeus in place of this and calls him Thaddai. In the Gospel of Luke he puts in their place Judas son of James. Then they agree on Simon the Cananaean. Luke says: "the one called the Zealot." And Judas Iscariot, who betrayed him, that is, pointed him out on the night in which the Jews claimed to have seized him. These are the twelve apostles whom Jesus sent out. In the Gospel of Mark: "He called the twelve and began to send them out two by two, and gave them authority over unclean spirits," saying: "Do not go on the road of the Gentiles, and do not enter a city of the Samaritans, but go rather to the lost sheep of the house of Israel. As you go, preach and say: 'The kingdom of heaven has drawn near.' Heal the sick, raise the dead, cleanse the lepers, cast out demons. Freely you have received, freely give. Do not acquire gold, silver or copper in your belts, nor a wallet for the road, nor two tunics, nor sandals, nor a staff, for the worker deserves his food." (p-50) In the Gospel of Mark: "He commanded them to take nothing on the road except a staff alone, no wallet, no bread, no silver, no copper in their belts, but sandals on their feet, and not to wear two tunics." In the Gospel of Luke: "He said to them: 'Take nothing on the road, neither staff, nor wallet, nor bread, nor silver, and you shall not have two tunics. Whatever city or village you enter, inquire there who is worthy of you, and remain there until you leave. When you enter a house, greet it. If the house is worthy of your peace, your peace will rest upon it; if it is not worthy, your peace will return to you. Whoever does not receive you or hear your words, when you leave that house, that village or that city, shake off the dust from your feet.'" In the Gospel of Mark: "He said to them: 'Wherever you enter a house, stay there until you leave from it. And wherever a place does not receive you or hear from you, when you leave from there, shake off the dust that is under your feet as a testimony against them. Truly I tell you, the land of Sodom and Gomorrah will have more ease on the Day of Judgment than that city. Behold, I send you like sheep among wolves. Be wise as serpents and innocent as doves. Beware of men, for they will deliver you to the councils, and in their synagogues they will beat you, and they will bring you before governors and kings for a testimony to them and to the Gentiles,'" (p-51) and in the Gospel of Mark: "as a testimony against them and against all the Gentiles. It must first be that the Gospel is preached. When they hand you over, do not worry about what you will say," and in the Gospel of Mark: "nor about what you will answer. For you will be given in that hour what you should speak, and it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father," and in the Gospel of Mark: "but the Holy Spirit speaks in them." "And brother will deliver up brother to death, and the father his son, and children will rise against parents and kill them. You will be hated by all because of my name. Whoever endures to the end will be saved. When they persecute you in this city, flee to another. Truly, truly I tell you, you will not finish with the cities of Israel until the Son of Man comes. A disciple is not above his teacher, nor a servant above his master. It is enough for the disciple to be like his teacher, and the servant like his master. If they have called the master of the house Beelzebul, how much more his household! So do not fear them, for there is nothing hidden that will not be revealed, nor anything secret that will not be known. What I tell you in the darkness, speak in the light; and what you hear in your ears, proclaim upon the housetops. (p-52) Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul; rather fear the one who can destroy both soul and body in Gehenna. Are not two sparrows sold for a farthing, and not one of them falls to the ground without your Father's will? As for you, the hairs of your heads are all numbered. So do not fear; you are better than many sparrows. Do not think that I came to bring peace on earth; I came not to bring peace but a sword. I came to set a man against his father, a daughter against her mother, and a bride against her mother-in-law, and a man's enemies will be the members of his household. Whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me. Whoever finds his soul will lose it, and whoever loses his soul for my sake will find it. Whoever receives you receives me, and whoever receives me receives the one who sent me. Whoever receives a prophet in the name of a prophet will receive a prophet's reward, and whoever receives a righteous man in the name of a righteous man will receive a righteous man's reward. Whoever gives one of these little ones a cup of cold water only in the name of a disciple, truly I tell you, his reward will not be lost." When Jesus had finished his command to his twelve disciples, he departed from there to teach and preach (p-53) in their cities.

In the Gospel of Mark: "When they went out, that is, the apostles, they preached repentance, cast out many demons, and anointed many sick people with oil, and they were healed." In the Gospel of Luke: "After this also the Lord appointed seventy others and sent them two by two before his face into every city and place where he was about to come, and he said to them: 'The harvest is plentiful and the workers are few; ask the Lord of the harvest to send out workers for his harvest.'" In the Gospel of Matthew, what appears to be the meaning is that this speech was addressed to the twelve, for he said before mentioning their number: "When he saw the crowd, he had compassion on them, because they were lost and cast down like sheep without a shepherd. Then he said to his twelve disciples," and so on to the end of what I quoted from him first. This is reconciled by saying he said it to both groups. He returned to the first context: "Go, behold, I send you like sheep among wolves. Take no purse, nor sandals, nor a bag, and do not greet anyone on the road. Whatever house you enter, first say: 'Peace to the people of this house.' If there is a son of peace there, your peace will rest on him, and if not, your peace will return to you. Remain in that house, eat and drink from what they have, for the worker deserves his wages. Do not move from house to house. Whatever city you enter and its people receive you, eat what is set before you, heal the sick there, and say to them: 'The kingdom of God has drawn near.' Whatever city you enter and its people do not receive you, go out into its streets and say: 'We wipe off for you the dust that clung to our feet from your city, but know that the kingdom of God has drawn near. I tell you that Sodom will have more ease on that day than that city.' Woe to you, Chorazin! Woe to you, Bethsaida! For if the mighty works done in you had been done in Tyre and Sidon, they would have sat and repented in sackcloth and ashes. But for Tyre and Sidon there will be more ease at the judgment than for you. And you, Capernaum, will you be exalted to heaven? You will be brought down to Hades. Whoever hears you hears me, and whoever rejects you rejects me, and [whoever rejects me] rejects the one who sent me." The seventy returned with joy, saying: "Lord! Even the demons submit to us in your name, Lord." He said to them: "I saw Satan fall from heaven like lightning. Behold, I have given you authority (p-55) to tread on serpents and scorpions and over all the power of the enemy, and nothing will harm you. But do not rejoice in this, that the spirits submit to you; rejoice rather that your names are written in the heavens." In that hour Jesus rejoiced in the Spirit and turned to his disciples privately and said: "Blessed are the eyes that see what you see! I tell you, many prophets and kings desired to see what you see, but did not see it, and to hear what you hear, but did not hear it."

In the Gospel of Matthew, after the Jews claimed to have crucified him, he appeared to his eleven disciples, namely those who went before, other than Judas Iscariot who betrayed him, in Galilee on the mountain where Jesus had commanded them, and he spoke to them, saying: "All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me. Go therefore and make disciples of all nations." In the last part of the Gospel of Mark, he appeared to them while they were gathered together, and in those days they were weeping and mourning. He rebuked them for their little faith and hardness of heart and said to them: "Go into all the world and preach the Gospel to all creation. Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved, and whoever does not believe will be condemned. These signs will follow those who believe: they will cast out demons [in my name], speak with new tongues, take up serpents in their hands and not be harmed, drink deadly poison and it will not harm them, and lay hands on the sick and they will recover." After Jesus had spoken to them, he was taken up into heaven, and those men went out preaching everywhere.

In the Gospel of Luke: "When they went out, they went through the villages preaching the good news and healing in every place." At its end, after he mentioned his eleven disciples and the discourse they were discussing after the Jews' claim to have crucified him: "While they were talking, Jesus stood among them and said to them: 'Peace be with you. It is I! Do not be afraid.' They were startled and thought they saw a spirit. He said: 'Why are you troubled, and why do doubts arise in your hearts? See my hands and my feet, for it is I! Touch me and see, for a spirit does not have flesh and bones as you see that I have.' When he said this, he showed them his hands and feet, and while they were still disbelieving for joy, he said to them: 'Do you have anything here to eat?' They gave him a piece of broiled fish and some honeycomb. He took it and ate before them, and he took what was left and gave it to them. He said to them: 'These are the words I spoke to you while I was with you, that everything written about me in the Law of Moses, the Prophets and the Psalms must be fulfilled.' Then he opened their minds to understand, and said to them: 'Stay in the city of Jerusalem until you are clothed with power from on high.' Then he led them out as far as Bethany, lifted up his hands and blessed them. While he was blessing them, he parted from them and was carried up into heaven before them. They returned to Jerusalem with great joy, and they were continually praising and blessing God."

End of what I have quoted from the Gospels. Whatever wording in them gives an impression of deficiency has already been noted at the beginning of Surat Al 'Imran: it is not permissible in our law to apply it to God Most High, although its application was valid in their law. It is interpreted figuratively (ta'wil) and has been abrogated (naskh).

The Imam Muhyi al-Sunnah al-Baghawi said in his tafsir (exegesis) of Surat Al 'Imran, citing Wahb: "When seven days had passed, that is, since the Jews claimed to have crucified him, God Most High said to Jesus, peace be upon him: 'Descend upon Mary Magdalene on her mountain, for no one has wept for you as she has wept, and no one has grieved for you as she has grieved. Then gather the disciples for yourself, and send them out into the earth as callers to God Most High.' God Most High caused him to descend upon her, and the mountain blazed with light when he descended. She gathered the disciples for him, and he sent them out into the earth as callers, then God raised him up to Himself. That night is the one in which the Christians became smoke-blackened (?). When the disciples awoke, each one spoke in the language of the people to whom Jesus, peace be upon him, had sent him. This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿And they schemed, and God schemed, and God is the best of schemers﴾ [Al 'Imran: 54]. This is what has been mentioned about the apostles of Jesus, peace be upon him, that they were callers to God."

And as for the Messenger of the Prophet (ﷺ), they were conveyors of his letters (ﷺ). Whoever accepted that had his portion from Allah, and whoever refused, his answer was the sword that would obliterate his dynasty. I have set this out in full in my commentary on my versified *Sirah* (*Nazm lil-Sirah*), and it is mentioned in *Futuh al-Buldan*. [p-58] When the Prophet (ﷺ) sent his messengers, he adopted a seal (*khatam*) for the purpose of corresponding with kings. Abu Ya'la related in his *Musnad*, from Anas (may Allah be pleased with him), that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) wrote to Kisra and Caesar, and in another narration, to Ukaydir of Dumah and to every tyrant, calling them to Allah.

Al-Shaykhan (al-Bukhari and Muslim) related in their *Sahih*, and this is the wording of Muslim, from Anas ibn Malik, also (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: "When the Prophet (ﷺ) wished to write to the Romans (and in another narration, to the non-Arabs), they said: 'They do not read a letter unless it is sealed.' So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) made a seal of silver, as though I can still see its whiteness on the hand of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Its engraving was: (Muhammad Messenger of Allah). He sent Dihyah ibn Khalifah al-Kalbi (may Allah be pleased with him) to Caesar, king of the Romans, and instructed him to deliver the letter to the governor of Busra so that he might convey it to him. Caesar glorified the letter of the Prophet (ﷺ), accepted it, read it, placed it on a cushion, and knew of his truthfulness (ﷺ) and that he would overcome his kingdom. He gathered the Romans and commanded them to embrace Islam, but they refused. He feared them and said: 'I only wanted to test you.' Then Allah did not decree Islam for him, and Allah removed his rule from al-Sham, and from many of the Romans at the hands of Abu Bakr, 'Umar and 'Uthman (may Allah be pleased with them)." [Then] from many of the Romans also at the hands of those who came after them, and it established Islam there. But Allah rewarded him for glorifying the letter of the Prophet (ﷺ) by preserving his kingdom in the outlying parts of his lands until now. It has reached me that the letter is preserved among them to this day.

He sent Shuja' ibn Wahb al-Asadi (may Allah be pleased with him) to al-Harith ibn Abi Shimr al-Ghassani, and al-Qudha'i said: al-Mundhir ibn Abi Shimr, the agent of Caesar over the borders of al-Sham, [then] to Jabalah ibn al-Ayham al-Ghassani. As for al-Harith (or al-Mundhir), he became angry at the letter and resolved to march against the Prophet (ﷺ) to fight him, it is claimed, but Caesar forbade him from doing so. He honored Shuja' and sent him back. Murri the Roman, his chamberlain, embraced Islam, having recognized the description of the Prophet (ﷺ) in the Injil. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The kingdom of al-Harith has perished, and Murri has triumphed." Al-Harith did not remain long before he died, and after him, in his place, Jabalah ibn al-Ayham al-Ghassani took over, and he was the last of the kings of Ghassan in the regions of al-Sham. The Prophet (ﷺ) sent Shuja' ibn Wahb (may Allah be pleased with him) back to him, and he returned a gracious reply to the Prophet (ﷺ) but did not embrace Islam. He continued to wait until he embraced Islam during the caliphate of 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with him), when he saw the manifestation of the light of Islam and the extinguishing of the fire of polytheism. Then he apostatized and joined the lands of the Romans, over a slap for which he was to be retaliated against. Glory be to the One who does what He wills!

He sent 'Abdullah ibn Hudhafah al-Sahmi (may Allah be pleased with him) to Kisra, king of Persia, and instructed him to hand the letter to the governor of Bahrain so that he might convey it to him. When he saw that it began with the Prophet's (ﷺ) noble name, he tore up the letter before knowing what was in it. 'Abdullah returned. When the wicked man's anger had subsided, he sought him but did not find him, so he sent for him, but he (Abdullah) had outrun the pursuit. When the Prophet (ﷺ) was informed of the tearing of the letter, he invoked against Kisra that he be torn to pieces utterly. Allah answered his supplication, scattering their unity and severing their bonds at the hands of Abu Bakr and 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with them both). Then Yazdegerd, the last of their kings, was killed during the caliphate of 'Uthman (may Allah be pleased with him), and the kingdom of the Persian emperors became like yesterday that has passed. Islam spread throughout their lands and the word of faith became manifest in them. Indeed, Islam went beyond their kingdom to what lies beyond the river (Transoxiana) and to the lands of the Khata.

He sent Hatib ibn Abi Balta'ah (may Allah be pleased with him) to al-Muqawqis, ruler of Egypt and Alexandria. He knew of the truthfulness of the Prophet (ﷺ) as Caesar knew it from the Injil. He honored the messenger, sent gifts to the Prophet (ﷺ), and returned a gracious reply but did not embrace Islam. So Allah destroyed his kingdom at the hands of 'Amr ibn al-'As, commander of 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with them both).

He sent 'Amr ibn Umayyah al-Damri (may Allah be pleased with him) to al-Najashi, who embraced Islam (may Allah be pleased with him) and said: "I testify that he is the Prophet, the unlettered one whom the People of the Book await, and that the glad tidings of Musa concerning the rider of the donkey are like the glad tidings of 'Isa concerning the rider of the camel (upon them be peace)." [p-61] "And that seeing is not more healing than hearing (a report)." He sent many gifts to the Prophet (ﷺ), and sent his son with his embracing of Islam, along with seventy men from Abyssinia. He said in his letter: "I possess nothing but myself and those of my people who have believed in you. If you wish me to come to you, O Messenger of Allah, I will do so." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) prayed over al-Najashi and asked forgiveness for him.

He sent al-'Ala' ibn al-Hadrami (may Allah be pleased with him) to al-Mundhir ibn Sawa al-'Abdi, king of Bahrain, and to Usayhit, marzban of Hajar, with a letter inviting them to Islam or the jizyah. The land of Bahrain is among the lands of the Arabs, but the Persians had overcome it, and there were many people there from 'Abd al-Qays, Bakr ibn Wa'il and Tamim. Al-Mundhir, Usayhit, and all who were there of the Arabs and some non-Arabs embraced Islam, and the Prophet (ﷺ) confirmed them in their office.

He sent Salit ibn 'Amr al-'Amiri (may Allah be pleased with him) to Hawdhah ibn 'Ali al-Hanafi, ruler of al-Yamamah, who was an agent of Caesar over his people. He read the letter of the Prophet (ﷺ) and returned a reply that fell short of the mark. It so happened that a monk from Damascus arrived to him, and he informed him that he had not responded to Islam. He said: "Why?" He replied: "I begrudged my kingdom." The monk said: "If you had followed him, he would have confirmed you in your position, and the good is in following him, for he is the Prophet (ﷺ) whose coming was foretold by 'Isa (upon him be peace)." Hawdhah said to the monk: "Then why do you not follow him?" He said: "I find myself envying him and loving wine." Hawdhah wrote a letter [and sent] to the Prophet (ﷺ) with a gift in its place, and his people became aware of it [and came to him], threatening him. So he sent back the messenger and remained in his Christianity. The Prophet (ﷺ) said, when Salit returned to him:

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 6, verse 19 (part 4 of 6):

"Hawdhah has perished, and what was in his hand has perished." When the Prophet ﷺ returned from the conquest [of Makkah], Jibril (peace be upon him) came to him and informed him that Hawdhah had died. The Prophet ﷺ said: "Indeed, a liar will emerge from al-Yamamah, claiming prophethood, and he will be killed after me." And so it was, as is well known concerning Musaylimah al-Kadhdhab (the Liar).

He sent al-Muhajir ibn Abi Umayyah al-Makhzumi (may Allah be pleased with him) to al-Harith ibn Abd Kulal al-Himyari, the king of Yemen. When the message of the Prophet ﷺ reached him, al-Harith said: "This Prophet had presented himself to me, but I was misguided concerning him. He is a treasure for whoever comes to him. I will consider the matter." His affair lingered until he embraced Islam upon the return of the Prophet ﷺ from Tabuk, in the year of the delegations, and he corresponded with the Prophet ﷺ about this.

He sent Amr ibn al-As (may Allah be pleased with him) to Jayfar and Abd, the two sons of al-Jalandi al-Azdi, the two kings of Oman. They hesitated, and their opinion wavered (p-63). Then Allah resolved them upon right guidance. Jayfar said: "Indeed, by Allah, this unlettered Prophet ﷺ has shown me that he does not command anything good except that he is the first to take it up, and he does not forbid anything evil except that he is the first to abandon it. He prevails without becoming arrogant, and he prevails without committing wickedness. He fulfils covenants and keeps promises. He continually looks into the secret affairs of a people, and he treats his companions equally in it. I bear witness that he is the Messenger of Allah." His brother also embraced Islam, and they both wrote to the Prophet ﷺ of their Islam. He spoke well of them and praised them well.

In the biographies of these envoys — by my life — there were other than what has been mentioned: wondrous narrations and strange stories of the signs of prophethood and the markers of the message. I feared that mentioning them would lengthen the discourse and that it would become tiresome, although they contain nothing that would warrant tedium. In my explanation of my versification of the Sirah, I have sufficed with what is brief in them, arranged in a beautiful order and a verse whose style, by my life, is sublime.

These are the messengers of mankind. As for the messengers from the jinn, al-Tabarani narrated in al-Kabir from Ibn Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both), concerning the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And when We turned towards you a company of the jinn listening to the Qur'an﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 29], that he said: "They were nine men from the people of Nasibin, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ made them messengers to their people." Al-Haythami said: "In its chain is al-Nadr Abu Umar, who is abandoned (matruk)." The generality of this verse in encompassing the angels (peace be upon them) is supported by the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿That he may be a warner to the worlds﴾ [al-Furqan: 1]. When you reflect upon the context of the verses that follow it, together with the end of the surah before it, you will be certain of this: ﴿That he may warn whoever is alive﴾ [Ya-Sin: 70], ﴿You can only warn one who follows the Reminder﴾ [Ya-Sin: 11]. For they are among the worlds, among those who have received the Qur'an, among those who are alive, and among those who follow the Reminder. The address of warning comes in the mode of predominance (taghlib), since mankind and the jinn are fit for it. Thus what is said is refuted: that the angels, despite their being in the utmost fear of Allah, and despite their infallibility, are not among those who are to be warned. What further clarifies this is the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And whoever among them says, "Indeed, I am a deity besides Him," We will recompense him with Hell. Thus do We recompense the wrongdoers﴾ [al-Anbiya': 29]. There is no warning greater than this. Indeed, Isa (peace be upon him) is of this Ummah, and among those whom the verses indicating the universality of the message encompass, without doubt. The Prophet ﷺ said: "By Him in whose hand is my soul! If Musa were alive, he would have had no choice but to follow me." Imam Ahmad, al-Darimi and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab (the Branches of Faith) related it from Jabir (may Allah be pleased with him).

The position of Ahl al-Sunnah (the People of the Sunnah) is that the messengers of mankind are superior to the messengers of the angels. The message of the Most Excellent, the infallible, was established in actuality to Isa, and by way of conditional statement concerning his life to Musa (peace be upon him). Allah, glorified is He, took the covenant of all the prophets (peace be upon them): if they should encounter him, they would surely believe in him. The Prophet ﷺ, who is the noblest of creation and the most perfect of them, was addressed with warning in more than one verse. Whatever is interpreted in this regard concerning him ﷺ, the like of it is said concerning them (peace be upon them) (p-65).

Among what removes dispute and repels the excuse of one who makes excuses by the warning is the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿That you may warn thereby, and as a reminder for the believers﴾ [al-A'raf: 2]. The omission of the object of "to warn" (tundhir) indicates the universality of his message. Attaching the reminder to the believers includes them without doubt, for they are among its foremost (ru'us) — peace be upon them. And the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿That you may give glad tidings thereby to the God-conscious﴾ [Maryam: 97], and other verses. So the universality of his message to them is an increase in honour for him, which is clear, and an increase in honour for them through their constraining themselves to obey him and adhering to what he has set for them of the works of his religion (millah), in obedience to Allah, the Exalted, as an increase in their rewards and elevation of their ranks. This is like what Abu Hayyan said concerning the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿So take what I have given you, and be among the grateful﴾ [al-A'raf: 144]: that in the command to him in this there is an increase of emphasis and the attainment of reward through compliance.

Qadi Iyad said in the Seventh Chapter of the First Section of the First Part of al-Shifa', concerning the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And when Allah took the covenant of the prophets: "Whatever I have given you of Scripture and wisdom..."﴾ [Al 'Imran: 81]: The exegetes said: Allah took the covenant through revelation. He did not send a prophet except that He mentioned to him Muhammad and his description, and took from him the covenant that if he should encounter him, he would surely believe in him. This is reinforced by what he said at the beginning of the First Chapter: It is related that the Prophet ﷺ said to Jibril (peace be upon him): "Did any of this mercy mentioned in the saying of Allah, the Exalted, ﴿And We have not sent you except as a mercy to the worlds﴾ [al-Anbiya': 107] reach you?" He said: "Yes! I used to fear the outcome, so I believed because of the praise of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, upon me in His saying: ﴿Possessor of power, with the Lord of the Throne, secure﴾ [al-Takwir: 20], ﴿obeyed, and trustworthy there﴾ [al-Takwir: 21]."

Muslim related in the Book of Prayer from Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him) that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "I have been favoured over the prophets with six things: I have been given concise comprehensive speech (jawami' al-kalim); I have been supported by awe (al-ru'b); spoils have been made lawful for me; the earth has been made for me a purifier and a place of prostration (masjid); I have been sent to all creation; and the prophets have been sealed with me."

As for the one who understands "creation" (al-khalq) as "mankind" (al-nas), on account of the narration in which it says "to mankind" — this is arbitrary. Rather, the reverse is more fitting, to match the verses. Whoever is not rational has been excluded from this generality by rational proof, and so the rest remain included in the wording. It is not permissible for anyone to exclude any of them from it except by an explicit text and a decisive indication that removes dispute.

Al-Qadi Iyad said in the Third Chapter of the First Section: Al-Bazzar mentioned from Ali ibn Abi Talib (may Allah be pleased with him): "When Allah, the Exalted, willed to teach the Messenger of Allah ﷺ the adhan — and he mentioned the Mi'raj and the hearing of the adhan from behind the veil — then he said: Then the angel took the hand of Muhammad ﷺ and advanced him, and he led the people of the heaven in prayer, among them Adam and Nuh." End of quotation.

Abd al-Razzaq related from Salman al-Farisi (may Allah be pleased with him) who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "If a man is in a desolate land (ard qayy) and the time of prayer arrives, let him perform wudu'. If he does not find water, let him perform tayammum. If he establishes the prayer, two of his angels pray with him. If he gives the adhan and establishes it, there pray behind him of the hosts of Allah whose two extremities cannot be seen." Al-Mundhiri said: "Al-qayy" — with a kasra on the qaf and shadda on the ya' — is the barren land.

Malik and the Six (except al-Tirmidhi), and Abu Ya'la, related from Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him) that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "When the imam says: ﴿not of those who have earned Your anger, nor of those who are astray﴾ [al-Fatihah: 7], then say: Amin." In another narration: "When the imam says Amin, then say Amin, for whoever's Amin coincides with the Amin of the angels" — and in another narration: "whoever's saying coincides with the saying of the angels" — "his past sins are forgiven." And in a narration in the Sahih: "When one of you says in the prayer Amin, and the angels in the heaven say Amin, and one of them coincides with the other, his past sins are forgiven." And in a narration of Abu Ya'la: "When the imam says ﴿not of those who have earned Your anger, nor of those who are astray﴾, those behind him say: Amin. The Amin of the people of the heaven and the people of the earth coincide, and the servant's past sins are forgiven."

The two Shaykhs (al-Bukhari and Muslim) also related from Abu Hurayrah, likewise (may Allah be pleased with him), that the Prophet ﷺ said: "When the imam says 'Allah hears the one who praises Him,' then say: 'Our Lord, to You be praise.' For whoever's saying coincides with the saying of the angels, his past sins are forgiven." And in a narration: "When the saying of the people of the heaven coincides with the saying of the people of the earth, his past sins are forgiven." Similar to this is what indicates the angels' following (ta'mum) our imams, and this is evident in being bound by our Shari'ah (law).

Ahmad, Abu Dawud, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Khuzaymah, Ibn Hibban in their Sahihs, and al-Hakim related, and Ibn Ma'in and al-Dhuhli decided its authenticity, from Ubayy ibn Ka'b (may Allah be pleased with him) that the Prophet ﷺ said: "Indeed, the first row is like the row of the angels." And more conclusive than all that has passed is what Malik, the two Shaykhs, Abu Dawud and Ibn Khuzaymah related from Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him) that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Whoever bathes on Friday with a bath of major impurity (ghusl al-janabah), then goes out at the first hour, it is as though he offered a camel. Whoever goes out at the second hour, it is as though he offered a cow. Whoever goes out at the third hour, it is as though he offered a horned ram. Whoever goes out at the fourth hour, it is as though he offered a hen. Whoever goes out at the fifth hour, it is as though he offered an egg. When the imam emerges, the angels attend, listening to the remembrance." In another narration: "When the imam sits, the scrolls are folded up." [And in a narration of Ahmad from Abu Sa'id: "When the muezzin gives the adhan and the imam sits upon the minbar, the scrolls are folded up, and they enter the mosque, listening to the remembrance."]

Their leaving off recording the people and their attentiveness to listening is clear evidence of the angels' following, by what al-Bukhari, Muslim and others related from Abu Hurayrah, likewise (may Allah be pleased with him), that the Prophet ﷺ said: "If you say to your companion on Friday, 'Be silent,' while the imam is delivering the khutbah, then you have engaged in idle talk (laghw)."

Al-Halimi said in the Fourth Branch of the Shu'ab al-Iman, in answer to what was raised against the saying of Allah: ﴿If mankind and the jinn gathered together to produce the like of this Qur'an, they would not produce its like﴾ [al-Isra': 88], that restricting it to mankind and the jinn does not prevent the angels' capacity to oppose it. His words were: "As for the angels, they have not united upon that, because if the message was not sent to them, the Qur'an is not a proof against them. Whether they are capable of its like or incapable — and they, in our view, are incapable — makes no difference." He said in the Fifteenth Branch, concerning the fact that among the kinds of his honouring is the prayer upon him: Allah commanded His servants to pray upon him and greet him, and before that He informed them that His angels pray upon him. So Allah commanded His servants concerning their Prophet with that, on account of the excellence in praying upon him, given that the angels, despite their separation from his law, draw near to Allah, the Exalted, by praying and greeting upon him — so that they may know that they are more entitled and worthier of praying and greeting upon him. These were his words in both places, and he did not mention any proof for that.

Al-Jalal al-Mahalli, in his commentary on Jam' al-Jawami', attributed something similar to al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab, for he said: "Al-Halimi and al-Bayhaqi clearly stated, in the Fourth Chapter of Shu'ab al-Iman, that he (upon him be prayer and peace) was not sent to the angels, and in the Fifteenth Chapter, [that they are] separated from his law." He said:

And in the tafsir of Imam al-Razi and al-Burhan al-Nasafi (p-70), there is the report of consensus (hikayat al-ijma') in the interpretation of the second verse — that is, ﴿That he may be a warner to the worlds﴾ [al-Furqan: 1] — that he was not a messenger to them. End quotation.

This is a statement of negation, as you see, and it does not stand against the texts I have cited, nor does it establish that al-Halimi held this view except because of his saying that the angels are superior to the prophets, as Imam Fakhr al-Din transmitted from him in the book (al-Arba'in), and Shaykh Sa'd al-Din al-Taftazani in (Sharh al-Maqasid) and others. None of the Ahl al-Sunnah agreed with him on that except Qadi Abu Bakr al-Baqillani. Just as he did not agree on the root, he does not agree on the branch. As for al-Bayhaqi, he only transmitted it from al-Halimi, and his silence on it does not necessarily establish his definite approval. Al-Zarkashi said in his commentary on Jam' al-Jawami':

This is a question over which a dispute arose between the jurists of Egypt and an excellent lecturer among them, who said to them: "The angels did not enter into his call," so they rose against him. Imam Fakhr al-Din mentioned in his tafsir of Surat al-Furqan the entry [of the angels], arguing with the saying of the Exalted: ﴿That he may be a warner to the worlds﴾ [al-Furqan: 1], and the angels are included in this generality.

End of quotation.

This contradicts what is transmitted from him concerning the reporting of consensus. Even if it is authentic, there are several points:

Firstly: consensus can only be reached by those with knowledge of the transmitted reports from the memorizers of narrations and the statements of the early scholars on it.

Secondly: this is a report that admits of authentication and weakening, since with its chains there is the possibility that it was transmitted from someone not relied upon, or that he (p-71) took it from someone in conversation and assumed good of him, or that an error occurred to him, and the like. So there is no certainty except after knowing the one from whom it was transmitted, the chain of transmission, and its support by what establishes reliability, so that it may withstand these many apparent indications.

Thirdly: it will come from Imam Taqi al-Din al-Subki that some exegetes said there was a sending to the angels. Imam Wali al-Din Abu Zur'ah Ahmad ibn al-Hafiz Zayn al-Din al-Iraqi said in his commentary on (Jam' al-Jawami'):

As for his being sent to all creation, what is meant is those among them who are accountable, and this includes humans, jinn, and angels. As for the first two, it is by consensus; as for the angels, it is a matter of disagreement, so where is the consensus!

This is on the assumption that this transmission is authentic, and how could its claimant establish that by it? I examined Imam [Fakhr al-Din]'s tafsir of the aforementioned verse and did not find in it a transmission of consensus. He only said:

Then they said:

This verse indicates several rulings:

The first: that the world is everything other than God, so it includes all the accountable among jinn, humans, and angels. But we have been informed that he, peace be upon him, was not a messenger to the angels, so it must be negated that he was a messenger to jinn and humans together, and the saying of whoever said that he was a messenger to some and not others is refuted.

The second: that the word "worlds" includes all created beings, so the verse indicates that he is a messenger to the accountable until the Day of Resurrection, and so he must be the seal of the prophets and messengers. This is his wording in most copies; in some of them:

"But we have agreed" in place of "we have been informed," and this is not explicit in a consensus of the Ummah, as you see. He did not specify the place to which he referred in the other copies, so let it be sought from its sources and considered. As for al-Nasafi, he is an abridger of him. And God is the Granter of success.

Then I saw, in the introduction to the book (al-Isabah fi Asma' al-Sahabah) by our shaykh, the hafiz of his age Abu al-Fadl Ibn Hajar, in defining the companion (sahabi):

Imam Fakhr al-Din had transmitted in (Asrar al-Tanzil) the consensus that he, ﷺ, was not sent to the angels, and this transmission was disputed. Rather, Shaykh Taqi al-Din al-Subki preferred that he was sent to them, and argued with things whose explanation would be lengthy.

End of quotation.

It is strange that Razi transmitted this, which is found nowhere else, while he himself said in Asrar al-Tanzil at the end of the second chapter of the third section, on inferring the existence of the Creator from the creation of the human:

The fourth aspect, namely in the honouring of the children of Adam: that He made their father a messenger to the angels, when He said: ﴿Inform them of their names﴾ [al-Baqarah: 33]. It is established that every honour that was granted to a prophet, our Prophet ﷺ has [its like or greater] of it. [He also said in his great tafsir on ﴿And He taught Adam the names﴾ [al-Baqarah: 31]: It is also not far that he is sent to those whom the warning is directed at from among the angels, since all of them, although they are messengers, it may be permissible to send a messenger to a messenger, as with the sending of Abraham to Lot, peace be upon them both.]

End of quotation.

You know the matter of Jesus, peace be upon him, after his descent from heaven. The summary is that his mission to them, may the blessings of God be upon them, is an excellent rank and a lofty, complete degree, permissible for him and fitting to his station, in accordance with the definitive texts for the generality of his message and the comprehensiveness of his call. The apparent indications of the Book and the Sunnah have indicated his possession of it, although its affirmation for him entails no problem in religion nor any prohibition in belief. So we have no right to dare to negate it except by a definitive text, as our Imam al-Shafi'i, may God have mercy on him, said in (al-Risalah), regarding the verse of al-An'am: ﴿Say: I do not find in what has been revealed to me anything forbidden﴾ [al-An'am: 145]. He said:

It admits of two meanings: one, that nothing is forbidden to an eater who eats it ever, except what God the Mighty and Majestic has excepted; and this meaning, when a man is addressed with it, the one that comes first to his mind is that nothing is forbidden to him except what God the Mighty and Majestic has named as forbidden. What is like this is what is called the most apparent of meanings, the most general and the most prevalent. And if the verse could admit meanings other than it, it would be the meaning that the people of knowledge are bound to hold, unless a Sunnah of the Prophet ﷺ, may my father and mother be his ransom, comes indicating a meaning other than it that the verse admits. Then we say: this is a meaning which God the Mighty and Majestic intended, and nothing is said as particular in the Book of God or the Sunnah except by an indication in them or in one of them, and nothing is said as particular (p-74) unless the verse admits that this particular was intended by it. As for what the verse does not admit, nothing is said of it that the verse does not admit.

End of quotation.

Imam Abu Muhammad ibn Hazm explained it in al-Muhalla, saying:

It is not permissible for anyone to say, regarding a verse or a report: "This is abrogated," or "this is specified in some of what its apparent wording requires," nor that there is an interpretation of this text other than the apparent sense of its wording, nor that this ruling is not obligatory upon us from the time it was revealed, except by another text which establishes that this text is as stated, or by a certain consensus that it is as stated, or by a necessity of sense that makes it certain that it is as stated. Its proof is: ﴿And We did not send any messenger except to be obeyed by God's permission﴾ [al-Nisa': 64], ﴿And We did not send any messenger except in the language of his people to make clear to them﴾ [Ibrahim: 4], and He said: ﴿Let those who oppose His command beware lest a trial strike them﴾ [al-Nur: 63]. Whoever claims that the intended meaning of the text is some of what it requires in the Arabic language, and not all of what it requires, has dropped the explanation of the text and dropped the obligation to obey it by his false claim, and some of what the text requires is no more deserving of being restricted to than the rest of what it requires.

End of quotation.

The people of the principles of jurisprudence said: the apparent [meaning] is what indicates the meaning with a probable indication, i.e., one that is preponderant; and interpretation is carrying the apparent meaning to the probable but outweighed meaning. If it is carried to it for a sound proof, or for what we think is a proof while in reality it is not a proof, then it is corrupt; or if it is carried to it for nothing, then it is play, not interpretation. [Imam al-Ghazali said in the Book of Love of (Ihya') in discussing whether the vision of God in the Hereafter is with the eye or with the heart:

The truth is what has become evident to the People of the Sunnah and the Community from the indications of the Law: that this is created in the eye, so that the word "vision," "looking," and the other words that occur in the Law remain running upon their apparent sense, since it is not permissible to remove apparent meanings except by necessity.

End of quotation.] Imam Taqi al-Din al-Subki said in answer to the question about the message to the jinn, which was mentioned at the beginning of the discussion of this verse, that I saw it in his handwriting:

The tenth verse: ﴿That he may be a warner to the worlds﴾ [al-Furqan: 1]. All the exegetes said in its explanation: "to the jinn and humans," and some of them said: "and the angels."

The twelfth verse: ﴿And We have not sent you except as a comprehensive [messenger] to mankind﴾ [Saba': 28]. The exegetes said its meaning is: "except as a general sending encompassing all people," i.e., not specific to some people. So the purpose of the verse is the negation of particularity and the affirmation of generality, and it has no implication beyond humankind. Rather, its strength in generality requires the absence of particularity among them, and then it includes the jinn. Had the purpose of the verse been to restrict his message to humans, it would have said: "And We have not sent you except to humankind," for the word "except" (illa) enters upon what restriction is intended in, so when He entered it upon "comprehensive" it indicates that this is what is intended by the restriction, and His saying "to mankind" remains without implication; firstly, because it is an inverted implication; secondly, because it is not intended in the speech; thirdly, because it has been said that "al-nas" (mankind) includes humans and jinn, i.e., on the view that it is derived from "al-naws," which is movement, and on this view it also includes the angels. Among the lexicographers who explicitly stated that "al-nas" may be from humans and from jinn is Imam Abu Ibrahim Ishaq ibn Ibrahim al-Farabi in his book (Diwan al-Adab). Al-Subki said:

The seventeenth...

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 6, verse 19 (part 6 of 6):

﴿It is nothing but a reminder to the worlds.﴾ [Yusuf: 104] The eighteenth (proof) is ﴿You can only warn those who follow the Reminder and fear the Most Merciful unseen.﴾ [Ya-Sin: 11], and similar verses, such as His saying: ﴿That he may warn whoever is alive.﴾ [Ya-Sin: 70]. Likewise His saying: ﴿A guidance for the God-conscious.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 2].

As for the Sunnah, there are hadiths. The first is the hadith of Muslim from Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him: "(And I have been sent to) all of creation (kafffah)." ("To creation...") is general and undoubtedly includes the jinn. It is not an objection to this that it is reported in other chains in Sahih al-Bukhari and elsewhere as "to the people" (al-nas) in place of "creation" (al-khalq). This is because that (version) is from the narration of Jabir, and this one is from the narration of Abu Hurayrah. Perhaps they are two separate hadiths. In the version with "creation" there is an additional meaning beyond "the people," so it must be acted upon, since there is no contradiction between them. Then it is allowed that the one who narrated "the people" narrated it by meaning and did not render it fully.

He said: This hadith supports the view of the one who said that he was sent to the angels too. This is not far-fetched: perhaps on the night of the Isra' he heard speech from Allah and conveyed it to them in the heavens, or to some of them. By this it is valid that he was sent to them. But being sent to them in general does not necessarily mean that all the branches contained in his law bind them. He may have been sent to them regarding some rulings, or regarding some matters that are not rulings. Or they may gain an increase in faith by hearing the Qur'an. For this reason it was reported concerning one who recited Surat al-Kahf: "the angels descended upon him like a canopy." Then he said, in the course of his speech: "Unlike the angels, it is not required that all these obligations be binding upon them, if it is said that the message is general to them. Rather, that is possible, and it is possible regarding some specific matter, as we have indicated before." End of quotation.

I say: It is not denied that rulings may be specific to some of those to whom a messenger is sent and not to others within a single law: free and slave, women and men, woodcutters and herdsmen, in relation to some acts of Hajj and other things whose enumeration is extensive. Allah is the Granter of success. Whoever presumes to deny the message to them, among the people of our time, without a clear text compelling him to it, is weak in intellect, unsteady in faith, wavering in certainty, and sickly in religion. Even if he were only relating what was said, showing approval of it, not everything that is known is to be said, and it is enough sin for a person to narrate everything he hears. By my life! The matter is as the author of the Burda said, and the Ummah received it with acceptance and rejoiced in it in gatherings and assemblies:

*Leave what the Christians claimed about their Prophet,
and praise him as you wish, and be judged by it.*

When he had established God's testimony to him, by confirming that he is truthful, and this might have given the impression that no one other than God knows this, especially since the disbelievers of Quraysh claimed that they had asked the People of the Two Scriptures, who claimed that they did not know him, He followed it, by way of resumption, with His saying: ﴿Those to whom We have given the Book﴾, that is, from among the Jews and Christians, by Our majesty, ﴿the Book﴾, that is, the one that combines the good of this world and the Hereafter, namely the Torah and the Gospel, ﴿know him﴾, that is, the truth which you denied when it came to you, and over which there arose a dispute between Me and you. They know it because of my description in their Book, which they do not doubt, and because they are familiar with the like of it in the miracles by which it was established, and because of the confirmation in this Qur'an of their Book and the disclosure of what they concealed of their reports, and because of its methods, which they do not doubt come from the niche of their Book, along with its additional inimitability. So they know this truth ﴿as they know their sons﴾, that is, among the boys, by their features and attributes, with a knowledge about which they have no doubt. You have placed them in a position of trust and made them like arbiters by asking them about Me more than once, and a group of them has believed in me and testified for me. So what is wrong with you that you do not follow them? Desire has become clear, and the veil has been lifted from your error. (p. 79)

Since most of them conceal that and do not bear witness to it, He said, in answer to one who asks about them: ﴿Those who have lost﴾, that is, from among them, but He omitted it for generality, ﴿themselves, they﴾, that is, because of that, ﴿do not believe﴾, that is, because of the decree of wretchedness that preceded for them, by which they lost themselves through deviating from what the sound nature and the upright reasoning call to. Whoever has lost himself does not believe, so how could he bear witness? This sentence has clarified that whoever among them does not bear witness is in reality dead or lifeless, because whoever's soul has died is likewise; rather, they are more wretched than he. That wretchedness has led them to distort their Book and conceal much of what testifies to my prophethood, so they became the greatest of creation in wronging, through lying in the Book of God, in order to deny the messengers of God.

Since the implicit sense is: they lost, so faith escaped them, because they did wrong by concealing the testimony, and wrongdoing was the cause of their loss, "Who is more unjust...?" was linked to this, indicating that they had altered their Book or attributed to Him what is not in it. So He said, placing the apparent noun in the position of their pronoun for this reason: ﴿And who is more unjust than one who invents against Allah a lie﴾, i.e., deliberately (p-٨٠) ﴿against Allah a lie﴾, like those who distorted their Book and attributed to Allah what He did not say, additions they wrote with their own hands with no basis, leading His servants astray from them; ﴿or denies His signs﴾, i.e., those brought by the messengers, such as the Qur'an and other miracles, like the polytheists. There is no one more unjust than them, for they will not prosper. ﴿Indeed, the wrongdoers will not prosper﴾, i.e., so how about the most unjust!

Since the meaning of this was that they are the greatest of liars, He indicated it by their lying on the Day of Gathering, after the veil is lifted, so He said: ﴿And [mention] the Day﴾, i.e., recall their lying against Allah and their denial in this abode, and recall what is more astonishing than that: their lying in the world of witnessing (ʿālam al-shahādah) when the covering is removed and the veils are lifted, on the Day when ﴿We gather them﴾, i.e., We assemble them with the greatness We possess, while they are averse and humiliated, ﴿all together﴾, i.e., the People of the Book, the polytheists, and others, along with what they worshipped. He pointed to the magnitude of that Day, its length, its hardship, and its terror by His saying, with the particle of delay: ﴿Then We will say﴾, i.e., by the greatness We possess, whose veils have been lifted for them and whose seas and depths have become manifest to them, as rebuke and reproach, ﴿to those who associated partners﴾, i.e., those who named something besides Us a god and worshipped it in deed, whether idols, ʿUzayr, the Messiah, darkness, light, or other than that, or by being content with associating partners, for contentment with a thing is itself an act of doing it, especially if it is accompanied by denying the one who is right and testifying for the one who is false that their religion is better. ﴿Where are your partners﴾, He attributed them to their pronoun because of their naming them thus, ﴿whom you used to claim﴾, i.e., (p-81) that they were Our partners in worship or in testifying to what leads to it. "Call upon them today, so that they may relieve you of what We intend of harm to you, or raise you from what We intend of abasement for you." Their question here may be posed while the partners are absent from them, or when they are brought before them; in that case the interrogation concerns what they used to suppose of their benefit, so their absence is as their absence.

When the report of them being other than what actually occurred on that day seemed unlikely, after the veil had been lifted from the terrors and the quakes and fears had appeared, He pointed to it with the particle of distance, saying: ﴿Then their trial was not but that they said﴾, meaning: the outcome of Our having dealt with them through this question and similar trials, which by their nature cause whatever they touch to incline and change from its state, even as it is shaken by their blows and convulsions, was nothing but their lying in that assembly. This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿except that they said﴾, persisting in what they were steeped in of the attribute of lying: ﴿By Allah﴾, so they mentioned the Greatest Name, before whose majesty the firm mountains crumble and by whose command the hard stones speak, the Name that comprises all the meanings of the Most Beautiful Names, many of which became manifest to them on that day. They reinforced this by mentioning the attribute that reminds of their upbringing and the continuous favour shown to them, so they said: ﴿Our Lord﴾. They were not content with mere lying until they swore, nor with mere swearing until they mentioned the all-comprising Name and the attribute that adorns the speech: ﴿We were not polytheists﴾. That is: their denial of you brought them to a point where they lie on that day, after the unveiling, in hope of what will not benefit them, as you see the bewildered, astounded person in this world doing the same. Thus it is a despairing of the success of all of them, the polytheists and the People of the Book. Or the meaning may be a rebuke and a expression of regret for them: that the outcome of their disbelief, to which they were subjected, in adhering to it, boasting of it and fighting for it, because it was the religion of their fathers, was nothing but their denial of it, their disavowal of it and their oath of dissociation from being religious in it.

The meaning according to the two readings of the accusative and the nominative in (فِتْنَةٌ, fitnah), by taking it as a predicate or as a single noun, is as follows. The meaning of the reading in the accusative (فِتْنَةً) is: nothing was [their trial] except their saying, that is, other than their saying the lie; that is, nothing was their trial except this saying. So this saying alone was their trial. Thus He negated from their trial and stripped from it everything other than this saying of theirs. The trial is therefore restricted to their saying of the lie, and the lie may be established for other than it, that is, they lie without a trial, indeed in a state of ease. This is exactly the meaning of the reading of Ibn Kathir, Ibn ʿAmir and Hafs with the nominative (فِتْنَةُ), that is: their trial was not anything other than their lying. Thus their trial was negated from everything except lying, and so it became confined to it. It is permissible that the lie be established in a state other than it, according to what has passed. This estimation is precious, rare to find, and subtle in its path. It will come, God willing, at His saying: ﴿And their prayer at the House was not but...﴾ [al-Anfal: 35] in Surat al-Anfal, where what is useful here is found, so refer back to it.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 6, verse 24:

Since this is among the most astonishing of wonders, He indicated it by His saying: ﴿Look﴾, and by the interrogative in His saying: ﴿how they lied﴾, and by the indication that they did it (p-83) while knowing, from what was uncovered for them of the veil, that it would not benefit them, by His saying: ﴿against themselves﴾. This is similar to His saying: ﴿They swear to Him as they swear to you﴾ [al-Mujadila: 18], the verse.

Since their statement here guides us to the fact that their associates had disappeared from them, so they gave them no benefit whatsoever, and since informing about the loss of what one was approaching eagerly and rejoicing in, while it gladdens his opponent and brings him grief, is more emphatic, He stated it explicitly in His saying: ﴿And lost﴾, that is, vanished, ﴿from them﴾, either literally or metaphorically, or both, considering two different times, so that it becomes a rejection: ﴿what they used to fabricate﴾, that is, what they deliberately used to lie about, in claiming their partnership, out of obstinacy against the clear proofs that stand opposed to it.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 6, verse 25:

When he knew that these verses had become so interconnected that they formed a single verse, and he concluded with the meaning of His words ﴿So they have denied the truth when it came to them﴾ [al-An'am: 5], which is a characteristic that had become fixed in them until it was manifest on the Day of Assembly, he mentioned the division of those marked by what that verse had caused, namely the turning away from the signs mentioned in His words ﴿except that they were turning away from them﴾ [al-An'am: 4]. It was as if it were said: among them is one who turns away completely. So He joined to it His words ﴿and among them is one who listens to you﴾, meaning, he listens with all his effort, as in the Sirah (the biography of the Prophet) concerning Abu Jahl ibn Hisham, Abu Sufyan ibn Harb and al-Akhnas ibn Shurayq, that each of them sat near the house of the Prophet (ﷺ) at night listening to the Qur'an.

None of them knew of the gathering of the others. When the dawn rose (p-84) they departed, and the road brought them together, and they blamed one another and said: "If your weak followers had seen you, they would have rushed to him." They agreed not to return, but then they returned for three nights in a row. Then al-Akhnas asked Abu Sufyan what he had heard. He said: "I heard things I recognised and understood their meaning, and things I did not recognise and did not understand their meaning." He said: "I am the same." Then he asked Abu Jahl, who answered with what showed that he knew of his truthfulness but withheld belief out of envy and obstinacy. This is what is meant by His words ﴿And We have placed﴾, meaning, while the state is that We have placed ﴿over their hearts coverings﴾, meaning veils, the plural of kinan, that is, a covering, ﴿lest﴾, meaning out of dislike that ﴿they should understand it﴾, meaning the Qur'an, ﴿and in their ears is deafness﴾, meaning a heaviness that prevents them from hearing it properly; for it prevents them from comprehending it, which is the goal of hearing. Thus they do not believe in what is heard from you because of this.

When He mentioned what relates to hearing, He mentioned what is apparent to the eye, expressing it in a way that covers hearing and other means of knowledge, and said: ﴿And if they see﴾, meaning with sight or with insight, ﴿every sign﴾, meaning of Our signs other than it, ﴿they will not believe in it﴾, because of the obstinacy and arrogance they hold in following the fathers and forefathers, ﴿until﴾ their final state in this sealing upon their hearts became that, even without understanding, ﴿when they come to you disputing with you﴾, meaning in actuality or in potential, and the limit is included. It was as if it were said in wonder: what do they say in their disputing? So He said, displaying the attribute that led them to that: ﴿Those who disbelieved say﴾, meaning they covered over what is evident to their minds, and this is the meaning of sealing. ﴿This is not﴾, meaning what has reached us, ﴿except fables﴾, the plural of sutur and asṭur, the plural of saṭr; and they are also the plural of isṭar and isṭīr with their vowels and asṭūr, and with the ending ﹰ-ah in all of them, ﴿of the ancients﴾. Al-Nadr ibn al-Harith said this, and the report of this verse confirmed his words.

﴿And they﴾ is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) relating to the agent (fā'il) of ﴿listens﴾ [al-An'am: 25], meaning: they listen to you, while the situation is that they ﴿forbid others from it﴾, i.e., from listening, or from following the Qur'an, ﴿and keep away from it﴾, i.e., they keep far from it, as happened with Abu Jahl and his two companions in their agreement to abandon returning to listening and what follows from it. ﴿And if﴾, i.e., and not (wa-mā), ﴿they destroy﴾, i.e., by their worship and their persistence in it, ﴿except themselves﴾, i.e., they cannot harm you, nor harm any of your followers, in anything that would undermine the purpose of your being sent, which is the manifestation of the religion, the erasure of polytheism, and the humbling of the corrupters. ﴿And they do not perceive﴾, i.e., they have no kind of awareness of what their situation leads them to. Rather, they are like cattle, and indeed cattle are in a better state than they are.

When he made their failure to believe in these signs lead them to a great degree of ignorance, which was a source of comfort to him regarding their claims in this world, namely their disputing with him (ﷺ), and concluded the verse with the severe threat you have seen, the soul yearned to know their condition when they are returned to God and the matter of what they were threatened with is revealed. So He informed His Prophet (ﷺ) that their condition at that time will be belief, (p-٨٦) when their affirmation of him will delight them greatly, and they will wish to follow him because of the humiliation that will overwhelm them and the disgrace that will encompass them. This will increase them only in harm, blindness, regret and anguish. It is as if it were said: "If you could see their condition at the lifting of the veil, which is the time of full disclosure, you would see them believing." ﴿And if you could see when﴾, that is, when ﴿they are made to stand﴾ at the gathering (ḥashr). The verb is in the passive because the emphasis is on the act of standing them, not on who does it. ﴿Before the Fire﴾, that is, near it, so that they may enter it, overlooking all the kinds of punishment within it, and this is more intense in its torment. Or [it means] ﴿before﴾ the bridge (al-ṣirāṭ), and the Fire is beneath them. Or it means they came to know its reality and the extent of its punishment, from your saying "awqaftuhu ʿalā kadhā" (I made him aware of such a thing) when you inform him of it. ﴿They will say﴾, wishing for the impossible: ﴿"Would that we were returned"﴾, that is, to the world.

Since the implied meaning, as witnessed by the recitation of those who put the two verbs in the subjunctive as a response to the wish (or one of them), is "so that we would obey," the phrase ﴿"and not deny"﴾ is coordinated with the clause. That is, "while we do not" or "and we would not," [namely] ﴿deny﴾, if we were returned, ﴿the signs of our Lord﴾, that is, the One who is good to us, ﴿and be among the believers﴾, that is, those firmly established in faith. According to Ibn ʿĀmir, who put the third verb in the subjunctive, the implied meaning is: "Would that we were returned, and would that we did not deny, so that we would be happy, and that we would be [among the believers]." According to the recitation of Ḥamzah, al-Kisāʾī and Ḥafs, which put both verbs in the subjunctive, (p-٨٧) the meaning is: "Would that we were returned, so that we would be happy, and that we would not deny, and that we would be [among the believers]." The meaning is: if you could see their being stopped and standing in that humiliation, defeat, degradation, shame, and their questioning and answering, you would see a dreadful and horrifying matter and a hideous, abhorrent sight. However, it is omitted to magnify it, so that the soul may go in every direction regarding it. Its omission is permissible because it is known in general terms.

Now when We informed them, in the reading with the nominative (raf'), about themselves, with what they wished for, namely the return (ar-radd), and the reading with the accusative (nasb) implied a promise, it is as if a speaker said: "Would that Allah provided me with wealth, so that I would reward you for your kindness," which leads to: "If Allah provides me with wealth, I will reward you." Therefore, being of the kind that admits of falsehood, He, glorified is He, turned away from it, refuting them with His saying: ﴿Nay﴾, meaning: the matter is not as they claimed, because this wishing did not stem from a truth established within themselves, from love of its content and its fruit. Rather, ﴿there has appeared﴾, meaning: there became manifest, ﴿to them﴾, from the punishment against which they have no strength, ﴿what they used to conceal﴾, meaning: [of] the realities of the Hereafter and their hypocrisy upon falsehood! And since their concealing of that occurred in some time, He said: ﴿before﴾, meaning: they claimed that it was hidden, when in fact it has no reality at all, and they hid what the Messengers displayed of its proofs [out of obstinacy on their part, though it is clearer than the sun at midday] by the awe they put on. Therefore they wished for what they mentioned. ﴿And if they were returned﴾, meaning: to the world, ﴿they would indeed return to that which they were forbidden﴾, meaning: of disbelief and the disgraceful deeds they were upon, and the concealing of what the proofs had made clear to their minds. ﴿And indeed they are liars﴾, meaning: in what they reported about themselves regarding the content of their wish, that they would do it if they were returned.

Al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 6, verse 29:

He emphasized their disposition toward disbelief by His saying, coordinating it with His saying ﴿they would have returned﴾ [al-An'am: 28], ﴿and they said﴾, meaning: after being returned, what they used to say before death in denying the resurrection. ﴿It is not﴾, meaning: this is not the life in which we are engaged, ﴿but our life of this world﴾, meaning: the one in which we were before that. ﴿And we are not﴾ — and they went to an extreme in the negation — so they said: ﴿resurrected﴾, meaning: after we die. And our seeing of what we saw before this of resurrection is only magic having no reality. The witnessing of resurrection did not benefit them; rather, it harmed them. This is a possible and apparent reading, but the more fitting one for the context of the verses before and after it is that this is a report of their saying to him ﵊ in this abode, coordinated with His saying: ﴿And they said, "Why has not an angel been sent down to him?"﴾ [al-An'am: 8], according to the first interpretation.

Al-Biqa'i's commentary on surah 6, verse 30:

The phrase ﴿And if you could see﴾ is connected to what precedes it. That is, they said this statement when I informed them of the resurrection, and it grieved you because of what they said, while in fact, if you had seen them acknowledging it when their Creator questioned them, it would have pleased you, given their humiliation and what their affair would come to. He expressed this in the present tense to portray their state. His saying ﴿when they are made to stand before their Lord﴾ is a metaphor (majaz) for being detained in one of the stations of majesty (jalal), in accordance with what the attribution of "Lord" to them requires. That is, the One whose kindness to them has been long and whose forbearance toward them has been great, so He displayed to them, in that station, what He displayed of rebuke, reproach and censure. He also made them aware, through the implication of the particle of elevation (ist'la'), of the attributes of greatness that belong to Him, glorified is He, such as majesty and vengeance, because they did not give thanks for His kindness in raising them. The context of the verse requires that the answer be: "you would see them overcome by awe, with no helper, and with such intense dread that they could not speak." It is as if a questioner said: the situation indicates this, as though it were being witnessed. Will Allah speak to them, given what the expression "Lord" implies? It is said: yes, but it is speech of denial, disgrace and humiliation. ﴿He will say: "Is this not the truth?"﴾ That is, what My messenger brought you concerning the resurrection and other matters, which you now see as signs of My greatness. ﴿The truth﴾ means the established matter, complete in its truthfulness, in which there is no illusion or magic. ﴿They will say﴾ — that is, when they are made to stand before it — ﴿"Yes"﴾, and so what He intended occurred. They added to what they had been commanded in the world the oath, and so they said: ﴿"By our Lord"﴾, that is, the One who did good to us in various kinds of goodness.
