When these verses established particulars of His knowledge and power, and their conclusion was knowledge of the wrongdoer and others, He followed them with exclusivity regarding what is more general than that, namely the knowledge of the **keys of the unseen** (*mafatih al-ghayb*), which no one reaches except the one who possesses them. For no one has knowledge of the treasuries except the one who opened them, and no one opens them except the one who possesses their keys and knows how to open them with them. Establishing this in this manner is a matter of *al-tarqiyah* (ascent, progression) through the stages of belief, from a complete degree to one more complete than it. So He said, linking it to the meaning of what preceded, which is: "Therefore all of that belongs to Him alone": ﴿And with Him﴾, i.e., He alone, ﴿are the keys of the unseen﴾, i.e., those by which no one perceives the unseen except the one who knows them.

When that exclusivity was the meaning, He stated it explicitly in His saying: ﴿None knows them but He﴾. Specifying the negation regarding them, and not regarding the treasuries, indicates what I have understood: that the restriction [in it] by (*lakum*, "for you") implies that it is permissible for us to say that to the believers.

When He mentioned the knowledge of the unseen, He followed it with the knowledge of the witnessed (*'ilm al-shahadah*), because purely rational propositions (*al-qadaya al-'aqliyyah al-mahdah*) are difficult to know completely, except for the perfected among mankind, (p-136) who have detached themselves and accustomed themselves to recalling abstract intelligibles (*al-ma'qulat al-mujarradah*). The Qur'an was revealed only for the benefit of all creation, the intelligent among them and the dull. So mentioning sensible things that fall under the universal rational proposition serves as an aid to conceiving that intelligible and firmly establishing it in the heart. Thus He said, confirming this universal, abstract intelligible with an example that falls under it and functions like the sensible. He linked it with the conjunction *wa* (and), as the linking of the particular to the general, to indicate its magnification. He said: ﴿And He knows what is on the land﴾, and He placed it first because a human being is more in contact with it, through what it contains of towns, cities, deserts, mountains, and hills, and the abundance of animals and plants in it, the *najm* (low plants without stems) and *dhu al-saq* (plants with stems), and minerals; ﴿and the sea﴾. He placed it last because the mind's comprehension of its conditions is less, although the senses indicate that its wonders are more numerous, its length and breadth greater, and what is in it of animals and kinds of creatures more wondrous. So this sensible matter served to strengthen the magnitude of that intelligible matter.

When He mentioned what encompasses both the fixed and the moving, He specified the moving, pointing to particulars and magnifying knowledge by magnifying the things known. He said: ﴿Nor does a leaf fall﴾, and He went to the extreme in negation with His saying: ﴿from a leaf﴾, and He made it indefinite to complete the generality: ﴿but He knows it﴾. Since this, despite its greatness, is apparent, He mentioned what is finer than it, saying: ﴿nor a grain﴾, i.e., and there is no grain (p-137) ﴿in the darknesses of the earth﴾, which indicates that the earth has no light of its own, alerting to what wonders have been deposited in this human being formed from it. That is, even if it is in the innermost part of it; so how much more so for what is in the light, and that is greater than a grain.

When He specified, He returned to generality, making the last refer back to the first, and He said: ﴿Nor anything fresh or dry﴾, i.e., whether it has existed, or has not existed, or will exist, ﴿but it is in a clear register﴾, i.e., one that makes clear its conditions, its essences, and all its affairs and times. Thus it is established that He is the Doer of the entire world, its substances and its accidents, in the manner of perfect precision and mastery, because He alone knows all that is knowable. Whoever is exclusively acquainted with the knowledge of all that is knowable is exclusively the maker of all made things, able over all that is possible.

Since among the keys of the unseen are death and resurrection, which they deny, and among their great proofs are sleep and waking from it, together with its repeated favour, and since in it, besides that, is an affirmation of perfect power after the affirmation of perfect knowledge, He followed that with His saying: ﴿And He is the One﴾, i.e., alone, ﴿who takes you back﴾, i.e., seizes your souls completely so that no awareness remains with you at all, preventing you from acting by sleep just as He prevents you by death. He mentioned the basis for this, saying: ﴿by night﴾ and ﴿He knows﴾, i.e., the state being that He knows ﴿what you have earned﴾, i.e., committed, ﴿by day﴾, i.e., the day that was followed by that sleep, of sins that bring destruction, and He deals with you concerning them with forbearance after knowledge and does not hasten against you. This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿Then He raises you up﴾, i.e., wakes you after that deep sleep, so that He disposes you in what He wills ﴿therein﴾, i.e., in the day that followed that sleep, after your having deserved retribution, ﴿that a term appointed﴾, i.e., may be completed, ﴿may be fulfilled﴾, which He decreed for the Greater Death (the death of the Hereafter).

Since, through this resurrection after that folding up in the Lesser Death (sleep), the power over the like of it in the Greater Death was established, and since in it there is a great drawing near to this, He said: ﴿Then﴾ He will raise you from that death as He raised you from this one, and ﴿to Him﴾, i.e., to Him alone, will be ﴿your return﴾, i.e., sensibly by gathering to the abode of recompense, and in meaning by the severing of causes as was customary in this world, ﴿then﴾, after those long standings, earthquakes and terrors. The particle of delay may indicate the greatness of the knowledge of that, and most of what precedes this in the context points to it. ﴿He will inform you﴾, i.e., He will tell you with a great, sublime and thorough information, ﴿of what you used to do﴾, i.e., so that He may recompense you for it. And because of His knowledge He expressed it with "doing," since the reckoning is upon those who are responsible and possess the capacity of knowledge. Thus there is established, along with His perfect power, glory be to Him, over the origination of these things and knowledge of them, His independence in preserving them in every state and disposing them in the best manner.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 6, verse 61:

When He had informed of the completeness of His knowledge and power, He informed of the overwhelming nature of His dominion and the greatness of His might, and that these His acts are by way of compulsion, so that none can oppose them. Were anyone to strive with all his effort to sleep outside his time, he would not be able; or to rise at the time of sleep, he would be unable; or to give life at the time of death, he would not be able... and so on through the rest of such cases. So He said: ﴿And He is the Subduer﴾, i.e., He does that while He alone, by virtue of what He has of the unseen of the unseen and the veils of majesty, is ﴿the Subduer﴾. He depicted this by His saying: ﴿over His servants﴾, i.e., in encompassing by knowledge and by action. As for His subduing non-existence, it is by bringing into being and originating; and as for His subduing existence, it is by annihilation and corruption, by transferring the contingent (mumkin) from non-existence to existence at one time and from existence to non-existence at another. Thus He overcomes light by darkness and darkness by light, and day by night and night by day, and so on through the other kinds of beings and the vicissitudes of contingent things. ﴿And He sends﴾ — and he returned to address (khitab) because it is more explicit — so He said: ﴿over you﴾ [He sends], from among His angels, ﴿guardians﴾, i.e., they guard over you every movement and stillness, so that you may be shy before them and fear the consequence of their recording. And [this is] so that they may establish against you, by their testimony, the proof over the courses of your habits; otherwise He - glorified be He - is free of need of them, for He is the All-Knowing, the All-Powerful, and they guard you according to His will concerning you. ﴿Until, when death comes﴾ (p-140). Since placing the object first is more frightening, he said: ﴿to one of you﴾, i.e., from which there is no escape or refuge, ﴿Our messengers take him﴾, i.e., they take his soul completely, ﴿Our messengers﴾ — from the Angel of Death and his helpers, despite their greatness in relation to Us, ﴿and they do not fail﴾ in a single breath, nor less, nor more, by neglecting it, so that it might advance from its time or be delayed.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 6, verse 62:

When He - glorified is He - indicated His power through the hosts, which are beyond counting, though He is independent of them by the attribute of subjugation, He drew attention, by using the passive form, to the summoning of His greatness, His all-encompassing might and His power, so He said: ﴿Then﴾, that is, after their being confined in the bond of the barzakh, ﴿they are returned﴾, that is, returned by a returner from Him whom they cannot resist at all, ﴿to Allah﴾, that is, the One whose greatness cannot be limited and whose hosts and servants cannot be counted, ﴿their Mawla﴾, that is, their Originator and the Manager of all their affairs, ﴿the True﴾, that is, the One whose guardianship is established, and every guardianship other than His, whether of the guardian angels or others, is non-existent; for the guardian angels know only what appears to them, whereas He - glorified is He - knows the secret and what is more hidden.

When the addressee had summoned to mind His might and subjugation, and imagined His majesty and greatness, so that his heart and hearing became fit for what is cast to him and recited to him, He said: ﴿Verily, to Him belongs the judgment﴾, that is, to Him alone in truth. ﴿The judgment﴾: since sole authority over judgment among all creatures is a matter that bewilders thought and hardly falls within the scope of imagination, He said, belittling it in comparison with His power: (p-141) ﴿And He is the swiftest of reckoners﴾, that is, He alone; He separates all creatures in a speed faster than a glance, just as He apportions their provisions in the world in a similar manner. No one can escape His punishment through prolonging the reckoning or through deceiving regarding reward or punishment, because He - glorified is He - needs no thought, deliberation, counting or writing. Thus no reckoning distracts Him from another reckoning, nor does anything distract Him from anything.

Since they acknowledged that the one who does that is Allah, but they were ungrateful for His favor, they were regarded as deniers. So He commanded him to give the answer without waiting for their reply, saying: ﴿Say: "Allah"﴾, that is, the One to whom belongs all majesty. ﴿He delivers you from them﴾, that is, from that hardship, ﴿and from every distress﴾ (p-143) that you have fallen into. How great is the placement of His words: ﴿Then you ascribe partners [to Him]﴾, along with the commitment to sincerity at the time of distress and the commitment to gratitude, indicating the improbability of their breaking their word through the particle of delay, together with the paronomasia in it, in relation to what they ought to have had, namely that they would be thankful.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 6, verse 65:

When they, through their association of others with God, were as though they thought that the hardship had departed from them with a departure that would never return, and it was fitting for them to remain constantly humble, either out of gratitude or out of fear, He informed them, as a warning to them of His might and an admonition concerning the extent of His power, that their hardship, the very one that had humbled them, had not in reality gone away. For the King's power over it in a time of ease is the same as His power over it at the time it occurs, since He is the Creator of both states, their causes, and what is in them. But they were blind of sight and coarse of nature. So He said: ﴿Say: He﴾, that is, Him alone, ﴿is the Able﴾. He did not give it the form of an intensive (mubalagha) because they did not deny His power; rather, they claimed the partnership that He negated by the restriction. Moreover, the definite article conveys intensiveness. ﴿to send﴾, that is, at whatever time He wills, ﴿upon you﴾, that is, in every state, ﴿a punishment from above you﴾, by dropping the sky in pieces or some part of it, like the stones with which He pelted the people of Lot and the companions of the Elephant, or by setting your great ones over you ﴿or from beneath your feet﴾, that is, by sinking the earth or by stirring up snakes or other things from the earth, as happened to some of those who came before, or by setting your lowly ones and slaves over you. ﴿or to confuse you﴾, that is, to mix you together, ﴿in factions﴾, that is, scattered, each faction following its own desire, so that this becomes a cause of the sword. ﴿and make you taste the violence of one another﴾, that is, the violence of some of those factions against others. In this He makes no distinction between the Sacred Precinct and other places, and plundering and raids become widespread. The way this statement is framed indicates that it is to occur at a certain time for certain people, since the speech of kings is protected from being without any form that could exist, even if it is in the manner of a condition or the like. How much more so for the King of kings, the Knower of the unseen! And to train one in this kind of understanding of the speech of God, the Prophet (ﷺ) said, in what al-Tirmidhi related in the Book of Tafsir from Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas (may Allah be pleased with him): "Indeed, it is going to happen, and its interpretation has not yet come."

He said: ḥasan gharīb (a hadith that is ḥasan and gharib). A fuller explanation and verification of this will come in His statement in al-Furqan: ﴿Blessed is He who, if He wills, will grant you better than that﴾ [al-Furqan: 10].

Since this was a great exposition, he indicated its greatness with the words ﴿Look﴾, and magnified it further with a question, saying ﴿how We vary the signs﴾, that is, We repeat them, directed in all the wonderful, beneficial, and eloquent ways, ﴿so that they may understand﴾, that is, so that their state becomes that of one whose understanding and benefit from it is hoped for. This was...

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 6, verse 66:

And the situation is that ﴿they denied it﴾, i.e., this punishment (p-145), or the Qur'an, which comprises the promise and the threat, and the causes that make clear to creation everything that benefits them, so that they may adhere to it, and everything that harms them, so that they may beware of it. ﴿Your people﴾, i.e., those who by right ought to stand by all your command and rejoice in your leadership. For when one of a tribe rises to leadership, the tribe is honored through him, since his honor is their honor and his nobility is their nobility, especially if he comes from the house of nobility and the mine of leadership. And when one of them falls low, the tribe takes the utmost care of him and conceals his faults as far as it can, for his shame clings to them. Thus this is a great rebuke to them and a subtle reproach. He increased this by his saying: ﴿And He﴾, i.e., and the situation is that He is ﴿the Truth﴾, i.e., the established reality which denial does not harm and whose removal is not possible.

Since a person may sometimes receive blame because of his people, he (ﷺ) in this station was liable to fear the consequence of that and to say: "What shall I do with them?" So Exalted is He, instructing him, said that there is no harm upon him from their denial: ﴿Say: I am not﴾. He placed the prepositional phrase first for emphasis on it, expressing it with the particle that indicates compulsion and domination, and so He said: ﴿over you a guardian﴾, i.e., a watcher and a supervisor who would compel you to turn back from what you are in.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 6, verse 67:

When they were on the verge of saying, mockingly: "Let it be so, and we will not concern ourselves with you," he said, threatening them: ﴿For every news there is a settled time﴾. He indicated the greatness of its report by his saying ﴿news﴾, that is, a report which I have informed you of from among these great reports. The meaning of ﴿mustaqarr﴾ (p-146) is a place and a time of settling, whether of truth or of falsehood; that is, the report must come to rest upon one of the two, and no report from among the reports is free of that. ﴿And you will surely know﴾, that is, the place where its great report comes to rest, by a true promise which admits no failure, even if its occurrence is delayed.

When He commanded him what to say in reply to their denial, He then instructed him about what he should do when they plunge into denial, saying: ﴿And when you see﴾ He addressed the Prophet ﷺ while meaning others, so that the admonition would be more effective, ﴿those who engage in vain talk﴾, i.e., who speak, ﴿concerning Our signs﴾, i.e., without reflection or insight, but following their own desires. This is like one who wades into water and sets his foot down without insight, in order to conceal the places of his steps, and without full choice because the water overpowers him. ﴿Then turn away from them﴾ by abandoning sitting with them, or by whatever takes its place. Since plunging into the signs indicates little intellect, He said: ﴿until they engage in a different talk﴾. Thus He judged their talk on other matters as well to be plunging, because it contains the worthless and the valuable, since it is not bound by the order of the Shariah.

Since Allah, exalted is He and to Him belongs all praise, has lifted the ruling of forgetfulness from this Ummah, He said, emphatically: ﴿And if Satan causes you to forget﴾, i.e., causes great forgetfulness, indicating that such a matter is worthy of not being forgotten, ﴿then do not sit after the reminder﴾, i.e., (p-147) after remembering this prohibition, ﴿with the wrongdoing people﴾. He stated the noun in place of the pronoun, for generality and to indicate the attribute that is the cause of plunging, which is being in darkness.

When this verse was Meccan, and they were at that time unable to denounce [the disbelievers] except in their hearts, He said: ﴿Nor is there upon those who are mindful [of Allah]﴾, that is, those who fear Allah and therefore do not deny His signs by sitting with the disbelievers, ﴿anything [of] their reckoning﴾, that is, the reckoning of those who engage in such discourse when they are stronger than them, ﴿of anything﴾. We did not forbid sitting with them because there would be a sin upon them in it, given this situation, ﴿but﴾ we forbade it so that leaving them would be a display of disapproval, ﴿a reminder﴾ to those engaged in the discourse, because of their shyness at troubling the companion, ﴿that perhaps they may be mindful﴾, that is, so that their state through this would be the state of one from whom mindfulness is hoped, so that they avoid engaging in discourse about the signs, out of honor to the companion.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 6, verse 70:

When he had made this matter manifest in the form of a prohibition, he repeated it in the form of a command, out of concern for it and to emphasize it, and he showed them another attribute, which is the ultimate of the first attribute, together with what was added to it of guidance toward deliverance from ruin. So he said: ﴿And leave﴾, i.e., abandon with any kind of abandonment, even if it is in the least of its forms, ﴿those who have taken﴾, i.e., who have burdened themselves in following desire by opposing sound reason and upright natural disposition, by taking ﴿their religion﴾ according to the pattern of the most frivolous of their worldly affairs. And since religion is a firmly rooted quality in the soul, and nothing among the states of the soul is more firmly rooted or more established than it, and it is the most noble thing a human possesses, while play is its opposite, nothing ends more quickly nor is weaker in its construction than it, he said, censuring them for having changed the intended purpose of this surah, which is from the proof of Tawhid, which has no nobler, higher, more precious, or sweeter thing in any respect, with that which has nothing lower, weaker, more destructive of manliness, or more calamitous: ﴿play﴾. And since it might be said that when play ends they return to occupying themselves with religion, he followed it with what motivates it, indicating that whenever they grow weary of play, they stir up the souls toward it through amusement, just as you see the dancer, whenever he slackens in his dancing, they urge him on by strengthening the amusement, or by moving from one art to another of its arts and a wondrous matter of its matters. So he said: ﴿and amusement﴾, i.e., in mocking the true religion, through whistling and clapping, through the baheera and the saiba, and other such things. So do not concern yourself with them, and do not let your heart be preoccupied with them. ﴿And the worldly life has deceived them﴾, i.e., it has deluded them, ﴿the worldly life﴾, of which they are among the people most knowledgeable about its passing away, and that everyone in it is perishing. So their being favored with the blessings with which He—glory be to Him—favored them is in matters they can attain no happiness in except by following His commands and avoiding His prohibitions.

And since this might be understood as abandoning them in every state, he negated that with His saying: ﴿And remind by it﴾, i.e., by the recitation of the verses, which are the Qur'an, whose revelation is continually renewed, (p-149) and the pronoun in reality refers to the verses. That is: let them do what they wish; do not concern yourself with any of that, and do not abandon admonishing them with this Qur'an. That is, your duty is only to deliver the message; we have not burdened you in this state with more than that. ﴿Lest a soul be given up﴾. Al-Baghawi said in (al-Mujmal): al-basl means the palm tree, and abslatuhu means I delivered him to destruction. So the meaning is: lest it be left and handed over ﴿to what﴾, i.e., because of what ﴿it has earned﴾ in its worldly life, being ﴿without, besides Allah,﴾ i.e., the One singled out with greatness, ﴿any protector﴾, i.e., one who would take up its support, ﴿or intercessor﴾ who would deliver it through his intercession.

And since ransom is among the means of release, he said: ﴿And if it offers every ransom﴾, i.e., that soul, in order to reach release, ﴿every ransom﴾, i.e., everything that is thought to be its equivalent, even if it were the most precious thing. (And since) the harm is the non-acceptance and not its being from a specific source, his saying ﴿it will not be accepted from it﴾ is in the passive voice. And since that certainly yields that whoever is in this state is ruined, he said: ﴿Those are the ones who are given up﴾, i.e., those who did these deeds far from goodness, ﴿who are handed over﴾, i.e., delivered up, ﴿to what they have earned.﴾ Then he resumed his saying: ﴿For them is a drink of boiling water﴾, i.e., it is the utmost heat by which what is in their bellies is melted, because of what they believed in the verses, what appeared on their tongues. ﴿And a painful punishment﴾, i.e., it encompasses their outward and inward parts continually, because of what became manifest on them of that after it had been hidden. ﴿Because of﴾, i.e., because of the cause of, ﴿what they used to disbelieve﴾, i.e., what they continually renewed of covering over the verses.

When it was established that no one other than God can avert anything from God in any way, neither the gods they claimed to be their intercessors nor any other, and it was proven to them, to the utmost clarity, that everything other than Him neither benefits nor harms anything, then His words were a complete rebuke to them: ﴿Say﴾, that is, after you have set out the proofs that no one has any authority alongside God, denouncing them and reproaching them: ﴿Shall we call upon﴾, that is, with the call of worship, and He made clear the worthlessness of what they worshipped, saying: ﴿besides God﴾, that is, the One who alone holds all command.

Since the context is the enumeration of blessings, ﴿Who created the heavens and the earth﴾ [al-An'am: 1], ﴿created you from clay﴾ [al-An'am: 2], ﴿feeds but is not fed﴾ [al-An'am: 14], ﴿and sends over you guardians﴾ [al-An'am: 61], ﴿Who delivers you from the darkness of land and sea﴾ [al-An'am: 63], ﴿God delivers you from them and from every distress﴾ [al-An'am: 64], He placed benefit first in His words ﴿that which neither benefits us nor harms us﴾, that is, it has no power over any of that, so that they would be utterly without hope of the party of God's following them. This is like a justification for His words ﴿I have been forbidden to worship those you call upon besides God﴾ [al-An'am: 56].

When He mentioned the absence of benefit in their calling, He pointed to the presence of loss in their hope, so He said: ﴿and be turned back﴾, that is, by returning to polytheism. He used the passive form because the reprehensible thing is the turning back itself, from whatever agent it comes. ﴿On our heels﴾, that is, we would proceed in a direction opposed to our aim, and so we would be in loss at every moment through distance from the goal. ﴿After God has guided us﴾, that is, the One in whose hand is all good and over whom no harm has power, to turning toward the destination; He granted us success in it and rescued us from polytheism.

When He depicted their state, He gave it an image, saying: ﴿like one whom﴾, that is, we would be turned back from the height of nearness to the goal to the lowest depth of distance from it, a turning back like that of one whom ﴿the devils have lured﴾, that is, they sought to bring him down from his rank, ﴿and they have removed him from the horizon of his goal to the bottom of his destruction. He likened his state to that of one who has fallen from a height into a dark pit, so that in the condition of his falling he is in the utmost turmoil, certain of ruin, and blind to any escape ﴿in the earth﴾, being ﴿bewildered﴾, wandering astray, unable to find his way and not knowing how to proceed. Then He resumed His words: ﴿He has companions﴾, that is, this one who has fallen has a number of companions, but because bewilderment has taken firm hold of him, he does not accept ﴿calling him to guidance﴾. He explained their call with the words ﴿Come to us﴾, while he has gone off into the wilderness following the devils, neither answering them nor coming to them, because he has been overcome in his own self and has been barred from admonition and from the leaps of return.

Since this was something they knew and had witnessed many times, and since they knew that the calling of his companions to him was the utmost in sincere counsel and goodness, and that if he followed them he would be saved, but otherwise he would perish with a destruction that could not be remedied, their answer was: "The calling of his companions to him is indeed guidance." He then made clear that it is so insignificant and trivial that one may say: "It is not guidance in comparison with this which they call him to," by His words: ﴿Say: Indeed, the guidance of God﴾, that is, the One who unites all attributes of perfection, ﴿is﴾, that is, exclusively, ﴿the guidance﴾, that is, not any other, unlike the calling of the companions of the one who has been lured away. Rather, that guidance together with rescue from destruction is, beside this guidance, nothing at all, because the true thing is that which conveys to the happiness of eternity.

Since the sense is: "Indeed we have been commanded to adhere to it and to abandon everything other than it," He joined to it a general command, saying: ﴿And we have been commanded, that we may submit﴾, that is, the command has been returned to us from the One who has no command other than His own, to do all that pleases Him, so that we may submit, by actually performing Islam, which is complete surrender, thereby abandoning every desire; and that we may establish the prayer, by performing it in all its outward and inward limits, thereby adorning ourselves with the noblest of adornments through its performance ﴿to the Lord of the worlds﴾, that is, for His beneficence toward everyone in everything He has created;

Then he explained what was commanded, as if he had said: "that you submit (aslimu) ﴿and that you establish the prayer﴾ for His sake ﴿and fear Him﴾ alongside that," meaning: do them not in a manner of mockery and play, but in a manner of God-consciousness (taqwa) and vigilance, so that what appears of them indicates what is hidden of Islam in the one who does good.

Since the implied sense is: "It is He who began your creation from clay, and then you are human beings formed [in shape], and who made you living, so by His power over the span of days you disperse," he joined to it His saying: ﴿And it is He to whom you will be gathered﴾, meaning: not to anyone else after your resurrection from death. Thus he brought up the resurrection, which they deny, because of the abundance of proofs he had established for His complete power, in a context indicating that it is something about which there is no room for dispute. The consideration that remains is what lies beyond that: their pursuit of falsehood justified placing them in the position of one who believes he will be gathered to someone other than Him, glorified is He, someone who has no power to requite them. So He informed them that the gathering is to Him and not to another, because there is no speech there apart from Him, so there is no bond between those gathered nor any support, as there is in this world. The sentence, along with that, serves as a justification for the command to taqwa. It has become clear that the verse contains ihtibak (a rhetorical device of mutual omission): he omitted "the prayer" the first time because its mention the second time indicates it, and "Islam" the second time because its mention the first time indicates it.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 6, verse 73:

When they worshipped other than Him, the Exalted, even though they acknowledged that He is the Creator of the heavens and the earth, they were in the state of one who believes that what they worship besides Him is the One who created them, or that it shared in their creation. Thus no one other than Him has the power to gather those in His dominion. The Exalted said, alerting them from their heedlessness and waking them from their slumber, restating the proof He mentioned at the beginning of the surah in another form: ﴿And He is the One who created﴾, that is, alone, ﴿the heavens and the earth﴾, that is, invented, originated and decreed them, ﴿with truth﴾, that is, for the sake of establishing the truth, despite their great size and the escape from enumeration of the wisdoms and benefits within them. You see that truth is not established in this abode, nor is it near to being established. Therefore it is obligatory for everyone who knows that God is Wise (p-١٥٤) and Aware that he must believe that there must be a resurrection of the servants after their death, as He promised, so that He may manifest justice among them, nullifying every falsehood and establishing every truth, and manifesting the wisdoms to all creation.

When He established that the establishing of truth is the intended purpose, He affirmed His power over it by His saying: ﴿And the day He says﴾, that is, to the creation and to everything He wills, in this abode and in that abode, ﴿"Be," and it is﴾, that is, He is, and it does not fail at all.

When He affirmed that nothing deviates from His command, He gave the reason, saying: ﴿His word is the truth﴾, that is, there is no word other than His, because most of the word of others is false, for one says something and what he intended does not come about. And since this was in the station of warning of His might, He said, repeating His saying "And He is the One to whom you will be gathered": ﴿And His is the dominion, on the day﴾. Since the intended purpose was to magnify the blast, He put into the passive form His saying: ﴿the Trumpet is blown into﴾, because the ties between creatures are severed, unlike what you see in this abode of the continuation of means. And His saying: ﴿the Knower of the unseen﴾, which is what is hidden from everything other than Him, glorified is He, ﴿and the seen﴾, which is what has come to a state in which the creation perceives it, along with it being a cause for what precedes it, of the completeness of power, as will come in (Ṭā Hā), God willing, as a completion of the warning, that is: nothing is hidden from Him of your conditions (p-١٥٥). So beware of His recompense on a day when the means are severed, and mutual support and cooperation vanish. He, glorified is He, follows His custom that whenever He mentions the states of resurrection, He establishes in it two principles: power over all possible things, and knowledge of all known things, universal and particular, for no one can resurrect except one who combines the two attributes. ﴿And He is﴾, that is, alone, ﴿the Wise﴾, that is, perfect in wisdom, so He places nothing in other than its proper place, nor without precision, and there is no one to repel His command; therefore resurrection is necessary. ﴿the Aware﴾ of all sources and origins, so nothing of the actions of any of the creation is hidden from Him, outwardly or inwardly, that He might leave them unaccounted for.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 6, verse 74:

Since the subject matter of these verses is the subject matter of the three verses with which the surah opens, which refute the doctrine of the Thanawiyya (Dualists), who are the people of Persia, the people of Abraham (peace be upon him), and since Abraham (peace be upon him) was known for his merit among all the sects, most of them being his descendants, such as the Jews, the Christians, and the idolaters among the Arabs, while the Muslims know of his sincerity toward God, Exalted is He, and his standing up to dispute with those who associated others with Him, and his endurance of harm for this, He, glory be to Him, followed them with His argument against them, refuting their doctrine and dismantling their proofs. So He said: ﴿And when﴾, meaning: recall all that has preceded for them, as evidence of Our exclusive creation and perfect power. How great it is, how majestic and how vast! Reflect on its wonders and ponder its subtleties and marvels, and you will find that no one can produce the like of it except God. And recall when ﴿Abraham said﴾, meaning: recall his words. The purpose of mentioning his time is to draw attention to the fact that this (truth) has always remained established and affirmed on the tongues of all the prophets in all ages. In this argument there is an explicit statement of what the opening of this surah had alluded to, namely the refutation of this doctrine, and this is connected to that in the most fitting connection! It is as if it were said: Then those who disbelieve in their Lord equate (others with Him): the idols, the stars, the light and the darkness. So, O Messenger of God, admonish them concerning this, by (informing them) that there is no disposer but Us. Tell them that I am the One who created them and created all that they observe of substances and accidents. If they take heed, that is their good fortune; otherwise, recount to them the argument of Our friend Abraham (peace be upon him) when he said ﴿to his father﴾. Then he clarified it in the reading with the genitive, with the words ﴿Azar﴾, and he addressed him in the reading of Ya'qub with a damma. Al-Bukhari said in his (Tarikh al-Kabir): Ibrahim ibn Azar, and in the Torah he is Tarah. End of quotation.

This has already been mentioned from the Torah in al-Baqara, so perhaps one of the two is a title (laqab). The people of that land, namely the Kaldaniyyun (Chaldeans), who are also called the Kasdaniyyun, with the letter sin (unpointed) in place of the lam, believed in the divinity of the stars in the sky and of the idols on earth. They made for every star an idol, and when they wished to draw near to that star, they worshipped that idol so that it would intercede for them with the star, as they claimed. So he (peace be upon him) said to his father, disapproving of him and drawing his attention to the evident corruption of what he was committing: ﴿Do you take﴾, meaning: do you burden yourself, contrary to what the primordial nature (fitra) calls to, by making ﴿idols gods﴾, meaning: worshipping them, submitting to them, although they have neither benefit nor harm in them? Through this disapproving reproach he drew attention to the fact that knowing the falsehood of what one adheres to does not require much reflection, but is rather something self-evident or close to it. For they deal with these idols directly, in every respect, and they know that they are made and not makers, and their multiplicity indicates the falsehood of their divinity, as is pointed to by God's words, Exalted is He: ﴿Had there been in them gods besides God, they would have been ruined﴾ [al-Anbiya: 22].

When he singled out for counsel the closest of creatures to him, he extended it to the rest of his relatives, and said: ﴿Indeed I see you and your people﴾, meaning: in your agreement upon this, ﴿in manifest error﴾, meaning: far from the straight path, ﴿clear﴾, meaning: very evident by the immediate judgment of reason, together with its opposition to every prophet whom God, Exalted is He, had informed, from Adam (peace be upon him) onward. So it is, in itself, evident, and it makes manifest the truth, namely that the true God is not to be but one who suffices those who worship Him; otherwise He would be in need of one who might suffice Him.

Since it was as if it were said: "We showed Ibrahim (peace be upon him) this insight into this bold matter of the falsehood of the idols," he said, connecting to it: ﴿And thus﴾, that is: and like this great-in-status insight, and he narrated the past state with his saying ﴿We showed﴾, that is: by sight and by insight, over the passing of time and the recurrence of months and years, to an endless extent, for himself and for his righteous descendants, ﴿Ibrahim the malakut﴾, that is: the inner dominion (malakut) of Tawhid, so that he knows that everyone who worships other than Allah, whether an idol or otherwise, whether from his own people or from others, is in error, just as he knew that about his people regarding the idols. ﴿And that he might be among the certain ones﴾, that is: those firmly established in the attribute of certainty in the whole matter of Tawhid, in relation to all its particulars, through what We showed him with his sight and his insight. So he reflected on it until he arrived at it, after knowledge of certainty (ʿilm al-yaqin), at the eye of certainty (ʿayn al-yaqin), indeed at the truth of certainty (haqq al-yaqin).

When celestial matters are visible to all creation, both near and far, and are nobler than earthly ones, then if their fitness for divinity is refuted, earthly matters are refuted all the more. So he presented to them the argument concerning this matter. He said, as a consequence of the aforementioned showing: ﴿So when the night covered him﴾, i.e., it concealed and grew dark. He made the verb intransitive, though it is transitive, to indicate the intensity of that night's darkness. For this reason he used the particle of elevation and said: ﴿over him the night﴾, i.e., the cover fell upon him, so it veiled the malakut (the unseen dominion) of the earth, and he began to look into the malakut of the heaven. ﴿He saw a star﴾, i.e., one that had risen. It is as if it were said: "So what did he do?" It was said: ﴿He said, "This is my lord."﴾ So it is as if, from his keenness of sight, he came with this statement, which is suitable to be either a declaration or a question, so that he would give them the impression that he was reporting. This would make the purpose more hidden and more effective in avoiding partisanship, and it would draw them more strongly to giving careful attention and would alert them to the place of error and to the acceptance of the proof. For a similar reason he concluded the verse with his saying: ﴿So when it set﴾, i.e., it disappeared after that appearance which had been a sign of authority. ﴿He said, "I do not love the setting ones."﴾ Because setting is a movement, and movement indicates the createdness (ḥudūth) of the moving thing and its contingency (imkān). We do not think that it could be supposed of him that he said what he said at first out of belief in the lordship (rubūbiyya) of the stars, because God Most High has already indicated the invalidity of this suspicion by informing that He showed him the malakut of the two horizons and made him certain. He attributed the matter to himself as an alert to them. He inferred from the setting because its indication of the cessation of its authority and the baseness of its station is more complete. He did not infer from the rising, because although it is a movement that indicates createdness and deficiency, it is in a general sense a nobility and an authority. The elite understand from setting the contingency, and the contingent necessarily requires a necessary existent (wājib al-wujūd) who originates it, who is the ultimate goal of hopes and the place of alighting for journeys: ﴿And that to your Lord is the final end﴾ [al-Najm: 42]. The average people understand from it the createdness of movement, so there must be reliance upon an eternal one. The common people understand that the one who sets is like one deposed, because his light and authority have ceased, and that whatever is like this is not fit for divinity. He also singled out setting because his people, the Persians, were astrologers, and their doctrine was that when a star is ascending from the east to the middle of the sky, it is strong and of great influence, but when it is descending toward the west, it is weak in effect. The god is the one who does not change. This argument is a proof that the basis of religion is built upon proof and not upon blind imitation.

When he showed them the deficiency of the small stars, he raised their gaze to something greater than them. He therefore linked to turning away from the stars, because of their deficiency, his saying: ﴿So when he saw the moon rising﴾, meaning appearing at the very beginning of its rising. Al-Azhari said: "It seems to be derived from *al-bazgh* (splitting), as if with its light it splits the darkness apart." ﴿He said, "This is my lord."﴾ This was his practice regarding the first.

Since the reflection that the star is a locus of change, through setting, had reached their ears and stirred in their hearts, he said, ﴿So when it set, he said﴾, emphasizing in the strongest way, ﴿"If my Lord does not guide me, I will surely be among the people who are astray."﴾ That is, the One who was capable of doing good to me by bringing me into existence and nurturing me, because He does not change and has no partner, by creating guidance in my heart. This indicates that guidance does not belong to anyone other than Him, and it cannot be taken to mean the setting up of proofs, since that was established before this, nor to mean knowledge of how to reason, since he already knew it. (p-161) ﴿I would surely be﴾, meaning by worshipping other than Him, ﴿among the people who are astray.﴾ So this was stronger than the first and closer to explicitly denying lordship to the stars and affirming that the Lord is other than them, along with gentleness and keeping the opponent far from what would provoke his obstinacy.

Since he had negated from the celestial bodies what might mislead the opponent, He said: ﴿So when he saw the sun rising﴾, that is, with his own eyes, ﴿the sun rising﴾, that is, at the rise of daylight and the shining of the light about which they made the claims they made. ﴿He said﴾, showing the inadequacy of what is greater than the light, namely that from which the light comes: ﴿This﴾, using the masculine demonstrative for the presence of a justification, which is the masculine form of the predicate, to magnify it and to distance it from suspicion, and as an early warning that the feminine is not fit for lordship (rububiyyah, divine lordship): ﴿is my Lord﴾, as he said previously. Then he gave a reason for this, to clarify the respect in which what came before differed, which had produced doubt, and so He said: ﴿This is greater﴾, that is, than what preceded it. ﴿Then when it set﴾, that is, it went down, so its appearance was hidden and its light was overcome, and the army of darkness defeated it by the power of the All-Knowing King. ﴿He said: O my people﴾, thereby stating explicitly that the speech was addressed to all of them, and he called out before the heads of the witnesses.

Since the hearts had become free of what was presented in this argument, which was impressive in its proof, and had prepared themselves to accept the truth, He concluded the verse with His saying: ﴿Indeed I am free of what you associate﴾, that is, of this and of other things, a fortiori. He thus stated the purpose explicitly, because there remained among the perceptible celestial world no star greater than the sun nor brighter.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 6, verse 79:

Thus, when he (Abraham) had refuted by this entire system of their belief, he manifested his turning toward the true God, and that the correct path had become clear to him through this reflection. The intended audience is them, but his presenting it in this manner makes them more likely to accept it. So he said, drawing a conclusion from what the rational proof indicated in the realm of the heavens and earth: ﴿Indeed, I have turned my face﴾, meaning: I have sincerely directed my intention, not inclining toward anything at all. By this he expressed complete submission, for whoever submits to something turns his face toward it. And he indicated its perfection and the uniqueness of its perfection through its originated creatures. He expressed it with (al-lam, "for") rather than (ila, "toward") so as not to suggest a spatial direction. So he said: ﴿to Him who originated﴾, meaning: for the sake of the worship of the One who split open and brought forth ﴿the heavens and the earth﴾. Thus he concluded the proof with what the surah began with, in His saying: (﴿Who created the heavens and the earth﴾ [al-An'am: 1]). And the most evident proof of what has preceded, that I have explained the term (hanif, "upright in pure monotheism") as meaning inclining toward the proof with ease and gentleness, in accordance with the habit of the primordial nature upon which God created mankind, is his saying after establishing this proof: ﴿hanif﴾, meaning: easy, gentle, soft, delicate, inclining toward the proof, not stiff, dry, or rigid in blind imitation, as is the habit of the coarse and dull. He emphasized his disavowal of them with his saying: ﴿and I am not of the polytheists﴾, meaning: not of you. But he made apparent the description that necessitates disavowal and generality, meaning: I am not counted among your number in any way that would bring me close to you.

(p-163) When he had presented these proofs refuting the error of worshipping the stars and the sun, which are more evident than the sun itself, he followed them with a report that they did not return to him, but rather argued with him. So He said: ﴿And his people argued with him﴾, [claiming] that they would not cease worshipping them, because they had found their fathers doing so, and that if he did not desist from speaking against them, some calamity would befall him from among the afflictions. This is among the greatest consolations for this noble Arab Prophet, upon whom be the best of prayers and peace.

Since it is evident that their argument after these clear proofs was in the utmost degree of baseness, having sunk below the lowest depth, He exalted the station above mentioning it, indicating that it did not merit being mentioned. He clarified his answer to them because of the many benefits it contains, by His saying: ﴿He said﴾, i.e., by a statement, disapproving of them and rebuking them: ﴿Do you argue with me concerning Allah﴾, and He explicitly named the Lord, the Supreme Great Name, in His saying: ﴿concerning Allah﴾, i.e., concerning anything that pertains to the One who possesses all the attributes of perfection, especially Oneness. ﴿And He has guided me﴾, i.e., He has directed me by decisive proof to knowledge of everything that is affirmed of Him and negated of Him. That is, since He is capable, He has clarified that He, exalted is He, has done good to him, so he hopes for His like of that benevolence and fears Him regarding the consequences of disobedience; for whoever's benefit is hoped for, his harm is feared, and whoever holds in his hand benefit and harm, guidance and misguidance, is, by the clarity of the matter and the manifestness of the affair, such that argument is not to be directed toward him (p-164). He followed this with an explanation that their worshipped objects are stripped of anything toward which aspirations could be directed. So he said, conjoining it to what is implied: "So I hope in Him and fear Him, because He is capable": ﴿And I do not fear what you associate with Him﴾, nor do I hope from it for guidance, misguidance, or anything else, because it is incapable. Thus He affirmed power to Allah through guidance, because it is more noble, and He omitted misguidance, due to its being indicated by it and by the indication of what is negated regarding the partners. He affirmed incapacity for their gods by negating fear, which entails negating power to harm. That indicates that Allah, exalted is He, is worthy to be feared. All of this is an allusion to them that the intelligent person should not oppose except one whose harm he is secure from; so they, in opposing Allah, are in the utmost danger, which no intelligent person would undertake. And the verse is of the type of ihtibak (elliptical balancing).

When he negated from himself the fear of their gods, ever, in the present and the future, and it was an evident matter in the true religion that faith is not valid except together with acknowledgment that the consequences are hidden from the servants and affirmation that knowledge of them belongs to Allah, submitting the keys of the unseen to Him and restricting them to Him, he said, making an exception from the cause of the negation, which is that they have no power over anything: ﴿Except that my Lord should will﴾ — the One who does good to me in a state of harm just as He does good in a state of benefit — ﴿anything﴾, i.e., of empowering them by themselves or by their followers; for He is capable of what He wills. If He wills, He makes the inanimate speak and gives it power, and silences the eloquent speaker and renders him incapable. So in reality I fear none other than Him.

(p-165) Since this was in the form of a conditional, and a conditional and what resembles it is by nature issued only by one who is hesitant, thus becoming a place for the opponent to hope for [something] in it, he gave its rationale with what removes this illusion, saying: ﴿My Lord encompasses all things in knowledge﴾, i.e., He encompasses all things in power. So if He wills to empower the incapable, He removes from it every obstacle to power and establishes for it every requisite of it. This is the fruit of the comprehensiveness of knowledge, as its proof will come—if Allah the Exalted wills—in Surat Ṭā Hā. The meaning is that I did not abandon certainty because of doubt in my heart; rather I abandoned it because of my lack of knowledge of the consequences, announcing that this is a rank fit only for Allah, whose knowledge encompasses all things. The strongest evidence for this is his following of it by rebuking them for their failure to be mindful, by his saying, showing the tā' of the tafa''ul form, indicating that in their natural disposition is the root of remembrance which restrains from shirk: ﴿Will you not then remember?﴾, i.e., let there be from you a remembrance, so that you distinguish between truth and falsehood by recalling your own end: that whoever is absent from his Lord is corrupted or nearly so, that these inanimate things neither benefit nor harm, and that they are your own handiwork,

Al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on Surah 6, verse 81:

He marvels at them for their supposition that he should fear what they associate with Him, saying in disapproval: ﴿And how should I fear what you associate (with God)?﴾ That is, apart from God, such as idols and others, although they have no power over anything. ﴿Yet you do not fear﴾ — that is, while the state of affairs is that you yourselves do not fear — ﴿that you have associated with God﴾, that is, the One who combines the attributes of greatness and the power to punish and to inflict vengeance.

Since it is for Him — glorified is He — to do whatever He wills, He said: ﴿of which He has sent down no authority﴾, that is, for associating it with Him. Since the situation was difficult, because it is the root of the religion, he affirmed the prepositional phrase and placed it first, saying: ﴿so for you there is an authority﴾, that is, a proof that would prevent Him from sending down His anger upon you. The summary is that he, peace be upon him, placed security in its proper place while they placed it in the place of fear, so he marvelled at them for that. It thus becomes clear that this statement, and the words of Shu'ayb, peace be upon him, in al-A'raf, ﴿It is not for us to return to it unless God, our Lord, wills﴾ [al-A'raf: 89], and His words, exalted is He, in al-Kahf: ﴿And never say of anything, "Indeed, I will do that tomorrow," ﴾ [al-Kahf: 23] ﴿except [when adding], "If God wills"﴾ [al-Kahf: 24], all come from one niche. Since the prohibited matter negated here is only the fear of harm from their gods, and the harm befalling an opponent of them through their followers or others is among the customary ways of God among His servants, the Friend of God, peace be upon him, restricted himself to the attribute of lordship, which requires tenderness, mercy, sufficiency and protection. Both matters occurred in his story: their enabling of the causes of harm to him by kindling the fire and casting him into it, and His mercy in making it for him "coolness and safety." Since the prohibited matter in the story of Shu'ayb, peace be upon him, was returning to their religion, he added the mention of the Greatest Name, which combines all perfections and is free from all deficiencies, which requires evoking majesty, greatness, singularity and the grandeur that prevents approach to the precincts of disbelief. And God is the Granter of success.

When it became clear, as the sun is clear, by what he established of proof that he is more deserving of security than they are, he said, as a consequence of what preceded, confirming it to them: ﴿So which of the two parties﴾, that is, the party of God and the party of what you associate with Him — and he did not say "which of us," for generality of meaning — ﴿is more deserving of security?﴾ And he definitively bound them to answer with his words: ﴿if you know﴾, that is, if you have knowledge, then inform me concerning what I have asked you about;

Then he connected to this, as an indication that they have no knowledge at all that would let them report on what they were asked about, His saying, starting a new sentence: ﴿Those who believed﴾, that is, brought this act into being, ﴿and did not﴾, that is, and affirmed their claim that they did not ﴿mix their belief﴾, that is, did not mingle it or taint it ﴿with wrongdoing﴾.

Since the meaning was "they are the ones deserving of security," he turned away from that phrasing to His saying, pointing to them with the distal demonstrative to alert to their elevated rank: ﴿Those, for them﴾, that is, exclusively, ﴿is security﴾, that is, because of the description of them mentioned before, ﴿and they are guided﴾, that is, while you are astray, so you are doomed, since you stand on the brink of ruin. (The Prophet's ﷺ explanation, in what al-Shaykhan, al-Tirmidhi and al-Nasa'i narrated from ʿAbd Allah ibn Masʿud, may Allah be pleased with him, of this absolute wrongdoing in His saying, ﴿with wrongdoing﴾, is that it refers to shirk.) This is the wrongdoing described as great in His saying: ﴿Indeed, shirk is a great wrongdoing﴾ [Luqman: 13]. It is an alert to the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them all, that this indefinite noun (tanwin) is for magnification. And because they were native speakers of the language, endowed with its nature, they were content with this and at ease with it. There is no doubt that the whole context is about warning against shirk, and that it indicates urging the disavowal (p-168) of shirk, both little and much. So the matter comes to this: the intended meaning is "they did not mix their belief with any part of shirk." Thus the tanwin in that case is for belittling just as it is for magnification. This is the use of a word in its literal and metaphorical senses together, or in its two shared meanings with one wording at once. And Allah knows best.

When Ibrahim (peace be upon him) had stood up to establish God's proof concerning monotheism and to defend it, and the implied sense (intended to alert the listener to the goodness of what has passed, and to urge him to reflect on it) was: "This is Ibrahim's (peace be upon him) dispute with his father and his people," [God] followed it with His words, enumerating the aspects of His blessings upon him and His kindness to him, indicating the establishment of prophethood after the establishment of divine oneness (tawhid al-wahdaniyyah): ﴿And that﴾, i.e., this, the great-in-stature proof which We have recited to you, is the argument Ibrahim (peace be upon him) used against his people, and He magnified it by describing it, saying: ﴿Our argument﴾, i.e., which by its indication deserves to be attributed to Us, because it is among the noblest blessings and the most glorious gifts. ﴿We gave it﴾, i.e., by Our greatness, ﴿to Ibrahim﴾, and We made him comprehend its reality and gave him insight into it. He drew attention to the elevation of its status by the particle of height (ʿalā, "over"), with (ātaynā, "We gave") implicitly carrying the meaning of (aqamnā, "We established"), so He said: ﴿against his people﴾, i.e., dominating them, prevailing over them, with the proof he set up standing against them. Then He increased the information about his excellence by saying, in a new sentence: ﴿We raise﴾, i.e., by Our greatness, ﴿in degrees whom We will﴾, by the power We have to do so, just as We raised the degree of Ibrahim (peace be upon him) over all the people of his age. (p-169)

Since his disputation with them was in accordance with the law of wisdom (qanun al-hikmah), concerning the higher world (al-ʿalam al-ʿulwi), to which they attributed the creation and governance through light and darkness, and since at the conclusion of his disputation with them was [the point] that, according to the law of wisdom, a true king does not humiliate his soldiers, so there is no fear for them, and since before that he had reasoned concerning the resurrection, which is the focal point of wisdom, it was most fitting that at the close of the verse he should mention the attribute of wisdom. So He said: ﴿Indeed your Lord﴾, i.e., specifically addressing His Prophet (ﷺ) by the name of Kindness (al-ihsan), as an alert that His withholding of the proof from whomever He wills is for wisdoms that He intended, glory be to Him; and in this there is consolation for him (ﷺ). ﴿is Wise﴾, i.e., He does not do to His party except what His intimate friend (ﷺ) expected of Him, of that which gladdens their eyes, either in this world, or in the Hereafter, or in both. ﴿Knowing﴾, so no one among others is confused for Him, and He acts toward him in a manner that accords with wisdom.

(p-170) When he indicated his high rank by stating that He had granted him insight into the proof, so that he was upon clear insight regarding his affair, and that he rose above the opponents through the elevation of degrees, He followed this with what indicates it and indicates His wisdom through His knowledge of outcomes. So He said, informing that He made him honored in this world, because (p-170) the noblest of people are the prophets and messengers, and they are from his offspring and progeny, and He raised his remembrance forever on account of his standing up in defense of His tawhid (affirmation of God's oneness): ﴿And We gave him﴾, that is, to Our friend (khalil), peace be upon him, by what We possess of greatness, ﴿Isaac﴾ as a son for him in old age, when such a child is not born to one like him or to one like his wife, ﴿and Jacob﴾, that is, a son's son. Glory be to Him began with these two because the context is one of favor upon the Friend, peace be upon him, and he was most joyful with his son, whom he was granted and was not commanded to part from, and with his son's son, from whose offspring were many of the prophets who called to Allah, and who were among his chosen ones. The greatest reason for beginning with them is that his sons purified the holy land, which was the place of Abraham's emigration and his chosen dwelling for himself and his offspring, indeed the one chosen by Allah for him and for them after him, through the aid of its purification from polytheism and the worship of idols. They called to Allah and illuminated the earth with His worship.

Since blessing is not complete except with guidance, He said, beginning anew and placing the object first so that the statement would include both of them: ﴿Each﴾, that is, of them and of their father, ﴿We guided﴾. Then He followed this with those who were guided, past and present, as emphasis, because this path has always been followed by the pure servants who called to it in ancient and modern times. It is as if He is saying: If you hold to your religion because it is true for you, then its falsehood has become clear to you, and the truth is only tawhid. And if you hold to it because of its antiquity, then this religion to which My messenger has called you, along with the clarity of the proof of its truth, is the ancient one to which Noah called you, and those who followed him from the pure among his progeny, to Abraham your greatest father, and those after him from the pure among his progeny, up to Jesus, and then to this Messenger, who is the supplication of Abraham and the glad tidings of Jesus, upon all of them be the most complete blessings and the fullest peace. So he is most worthy of being followed in terms of truth and antiquity. And if you hold to it merely for following your fathers, then there is no one among your fathers like Abraham, peace be upon him. I have recited to you in My speech, in which I established the decisive proof of your inability to produce its like, the proof of the soundness of its attribution to what he argued with his father and his people in refuting the idols that misled you. So he is more worthy among your fathers that you take pride in him. And Allah is the Granter of success.

Since it might occur to someone's mind that the guidance of each of Isaac and his son came through the upbringing of his father, He mentioned the tenth of the Friend's forefathers, who is Noah, peace be upon them both, to rule that out. Also because the context is the denunciation of idols, and he was the first to forbid their worship, and he is the most exalted of the Friend's forefathers, peace be upon him. So He said: ﴿And Noah, We guided﴾, that is, by what We possess of greatness, from among that crooked generation.

Since [the lineage] did not pass beyond him, and his time was some of the distant past, He retained the preposition and detached it from the annexation because of the great distance of their time from his time, so He said: (p-172) ﴿before﴾, that is, his guidance was only through Us, in a time when its people were in utmost misguidance and persistence in injustice, like the approach of night, the more its darkness extended, the more it became intensely pitch-black. He had long called them to Allah and nurtured them, yet few of them returned, to the point that his wife and some of his sons opposed him. For a similar reason He separated Ishmael from his father and Joseph from his father, peace be upon them, as an indication of each one's separation from his father during his life, and that none of them was preserved upon the ways of guidance throughout the duration except by Allah. Then He began those mentioned after this with the one through whose hands and the hands of his son a mosque was built, which is after the mosque built by Abraham and his son Ishmael, peace be upon them both. So He said: ﴿and from his offspring﴾.

Since the whole context is praise of the Friend, and those mentioned, except Lot, were from his lineage, and since taghlib (the grammatical convention of giving precedence to one group within a broader reference) was a common and widespread usage in the language of the Arabs, especially since Lot was the son of his brother and like his son, He ruled that the pronoun refers to Abraham, peace be upon him. The statement of whoever said that Jonah, peace be upon him, was not from his lineage is incorrect; rather he was from the Children of Israel, and he is one of those mentioned in the Book of the Prophets, and his account will come from the mentioned book in the Surah of ﴿As-Saffat﴾ [As-Saffat: 1], if Allah the Exalted wills. Abu al-Hasan Muhammad ibn Abdullah al-Kisa'i clearly stated in The Stories of the Prophets that he was from the offspring of Abraham, while his statement implies that he was from the Children of Israel, as the statement of al-Baghawi also implies in the Surah of the Prophets, peace be upon them (p-173). As for Job, it is narrated that he was from the lineage of Esau son of Isaac, peace be upon them. ﴿David﴾, that is, We guided him, ﴿and Solomon﴾, that is, the two who built the Holy House (Bayt al-Maqdis) by the command of Allah: David by its foundation and laying out, and Solomon by its completion and erection.

Despite this, they were not two kings. He followed them with one who resembled them in kingship or in ruling over kings: ﴿and Job﴾. He placed him first because of the affinity between him and Solomon, in that each of them was tested by the loss of everything in his hand, then Allah returned it to him. ﴿And Joseph﴾. Each of these four was tested and remained patient, and was enriched and gave thanks. Job, if he was not a king, his wealth was not less than the wealth of kings. Moreover, some of the students informed me, from the tafsir of al-Hakkari, as far as I recall, that he explicitly stated that he was a king. Also, the first two were the cause of the reform of the Children of Israel after their corruption and their rescue from the humiliation of the Philistines, and the remaining two were each tested with separation from his family, then they were returned to him: Job after they had died, and Joseph before death (p-174). Also, David, peace be upon him, shared with Abraham, peace be upon him, in that he was the cause of his safety from the king of his time, through hiding in a cave. That was because Nimrod son of Canaan claimed divinity and coveted it, and his astrologers said to him: "In your land this year a boy will be born who will change the religion of the people of the earth, and your destruction will be at his hands." So he ordered the slaughter of every boy in his region that year, and ordered men to be separated from women. Abraham's mother became pregnant with him that year. When she felt the pangs of labor, she went out at night to a cave near her, and gave birth to Abraham in it, and tended to his needs. Then she sealed the mouth of the cave and returned. Afterward she would visit him and find him sucking his thumb, and he would grow in a day as much as a month and in a month as much as a year. As for David, peace be upon him, when he killed Goliath, and Saul gave him his daughter in marriage and shared his kingdom with him, as had been stipulated for whoever killed Goliath, the people inclined to him and loved him. Saul envied him and wanted to kill him, so he pursued him, and he fled from him. He entered a cave, and a spider wove its web over him. Saul said: "If he had entered here, he would have torn the spider's web," so Allah saved him from him. And He followed him with Solomon, because although he was among the people of kingship and trials, he shared with Abraham, peace be upon them both, in the abolition of sun-worship in the story of Bilqis, may Allah be pleased with her. The story of Joseph, peace be upon him, in the abolition of idol-worship is famous in the words of the Most High: ﴿O two companions of the prison, are separate lords better, or Allah, the One, the Subduer?﴾ [Yusuf: 39].

(p-175) Since Joseph, peace be upon him, was among those whose word Allah exalted above the word of the king of Egypt, and strengthened the kingdom and its people through him and gave them life through him, He followed him with those whose word Allah exalted over the word of the king of Egypt and his people, and destroyed them through them both. It is as if some of their stories are in agreement and some are in contrast and antithesis. So He said: ﴿and Moses and Aaron﴾. Since the implication was: We guided them as recompense for their goodness, in their own guidance and in their calling others to guidance, neither the gift of ease nor the trial of hardship preoccupied any of them, He followed this with His saying: ﴿And thus﴾, that is, and in the same manner as We recompensed them, ﴿We reward the good-doers﴾, that is, all of them. In that is an indication of the high station of these people in this respect, namely that they were among those of ease that does not sate and hardship that does not weary, and despite that, they did good and did not slacken or weaken.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 6, verse 85:

Since those mentioned before him were among those whom He empowered over kings, he followed them with those whom He empowered kings over by killing them, so He said: ﴿And Zechariah and John﴾. Then he followed them with one whom the kings opposed but was not given power over, and whose life Allah, glory be to Him, sustained until He willed otherwise, so He said: ﴿And Jesus and Elijah﴾. Since these four were among the patient, He praised them in a manner that encompasses those before them, saying: ﴿Each﴾, that is, of those mentioned, ﴿was of the righteous﴾.

(p. 176) Then He followed them with one who had no connection with them or with the kings, and [He guided] through the two of them one who was among their own people. So He said: ﴿And Ismail and al-Yasa'﴾. This is if al-Yasa' is the son of Akhtub, son of al-Ajuz, the successor of Ilyas (Elijah), as al-Baghawi mentioned in Surat al-Saffat, that Allah the Exalted sent to Ilyas, who was of the tribe of Lawi from the offspring of Harun (peace be upon him), a horse of fire. He rode it, and Allah raised him up, cut off from him the pleasure of food and drink, and clothed him with feathers. So he became human, angelic, earthly and heavenly. Allah gave power over Ajab (meaning the king who had oppressed Ilyas) to an enemy who killed him. Allah then made al-Yasa' a prophet and sent him as a messenger to the Children of Israel, and supported him, so the Children of Israel believed in him and used to revere him.

If al-Yasa' is Yusha' ibn Nun, as Zayd ibn Aslam said, then the connection between him and Ismail (peace be upon them both) is that each of them was true to his promise. Yusha' was one of the two chiefs (nuqaba') who fulfilled [their covenant] to Musa (peace be upon him) when he sent them to survey the land of Bayt al-Maqdis, as indicated in His saying the Exalted: ﴿And Allah had certainly taken the covenant of the Children of Israel, and We raised from among them twelve chiefs﴾ (Al-Ma'idah: 12), and His saying: ﴿Two men from among those who feared [Allah] and whom Allah had blessed said﴾ (Al-Ma'idah: 23). Also, each of them was the cause of the settlement of the greatest land of Allah with monotheism: Ismail was the cause of the settlement of the honoured Makkah, and Yusha' was the cause of the settlement of the sacred town, as will come in Surat Yunus, Allah willing.

(p. 177) Since Ismail and al-Yasa' were among those through whom Allah guided their people without punishment, He followed them with one whom Allah guided, [but whose] people [were guided] through punishment, and whom He saved after the signs of it had come. So He said: ﴿and Yunus﴾, meaning: We guided him. When the offspring of Ibrahim (peace be upon him) came to an end, He concluded with the son of his brother, whose people went astray and were destroyed suddenly. Between the two stories of these latter two there is an antithesis (tibaq) in terms of destruction and salvation, and a correspondence (wifaq) in that each of them was sent to people other than his own. So He said: ﴿and Lut﴾. Then He described them all with a term that covers those before them, saying: ﴿and all﴾, meaning: of those we have mentioned, ﴿We favoured﴾, meaning: by what We have of greatness, with perfect knowledge and all-encompassing power, ﴿over the worlds﴾. So all these prophets are among those whom Allah guided by His guidance and who struggled for Allah with the struggle due to Him. The Exalted began with Ibrahim (peace be upon him) and concluded with the son of his brother Lut (peace be upon him), in this fine correspondence. It has also been said that Allah the Exalted destroyed the people of Ibrahim, namely Nimrod and his armies, after his emigration. If that is correct, the correspondence is complete in the destruction of each people: the people of [Ibrahim] and the people of his nephew Lut, after their prophet departed from them. Thus there is a correspondence between them, just as there is an antithesis between his story and the story of Yunus (peace be upon him).

Among the subtleties of this arrangement is also that Ismail (peace be upon him) corresponds to Nuh (peace be upon him): he is the fourth in the count of this series if you count it from its end, just as Nuh is the fourth if you count it from its beginning. The connection between them is that (p. 178) Allah spread humankind from Nuh, until among them was Ibrahim (peace be upon him), whom Allah made the father of the prophets and messengers; and Allah spread from Ismail the Arabs, who are the essence of creation, until among them was Muhammad (ﷺ), whom Allah made the seal of the prophets and messengers. Thus the one was a beginning and the other an end. Also, the figures mentioned before the offspring of Ibrahim (peace be upon him) and after it, namely Nuh and Lut (peace be upon them both), Allah destroyed the people of each of them in general, and He hid these [people] in the solid earth, just as He drowned those [others] in the barrier of water. And He made wretched with each of them his wife, as a clarification that the messengers, just as they are a mercy to some people, are a vengeance upon others; and that there is no salvation through them, nor benefit, except through good following. Also, the son of Imran (Musa) shared with Ibrahim (peace be upon them) in that each of the two kings of their times ordered the killing of boys out of fear of one who would change his religion and seize his kingdom. And just as Allah the Exalted saved Ibrahim (peace be upon him) and his nephew Lut (peace be upon him) from the king of their time who claimed divinity, so likewise He saved Musa and his brother Harun (peace be upon them both) from the king of their time who claimed to be a god, and He saved the offspring of Ibrahim through them both. So if you make Ibrahim and his nephew Lut, since he followed him, one unit, and Musa and his brother Harun one unit for the same reason, and you arrange the names of all these (p. 179) prophets in a single string: Lut with Ibrahim as Musa with Harun, then the four are the central link of the necklace. Between Ibrahim and Musa there are then seven, just as between Harun and Lut there are seven. And if you add to them the one intended in essence, the one addressed by these verses, the one commanded by His saying: ﴿So follow their guidance﴾ (Al-An'am: 90), his position in the string would be between his paternal cousin Lut and his father Ibrahim, and nine would be before him and nine after him. From Ibrahim to Musa there are nine, and from Lut to Harun likewise. So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was the central link of the necklace and its completer, for he is the tenth on each side. Through him guidance is completed and the perdition of the lost is made binding. This corresponds to the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ) reported by the two Shaykhs and others from Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him):

"My likeness and the likeness of the prophets before me is like a man who built a house, made it good and beautiful, except for the place of one brick in a corner of it. People went around it, marvelling at it and saying: 'Why was this brick not placed?' So I am the brick, and I am the Seal of the Prophets."

Al-Bukhari has a similar report from Jabir. This is along with its association with the one closest in rank and lineage among the possessors of resolve (Ulu al-'Azm), the subject of the story, Ibrahim (peace be upon him). If you make Musa and Harun (peace be upon them both) as one thing, they were a link from the other side. If you count from the side of Ibrahim (peace be upon him), there are eight between him and them both; and if you count (p. 180) from the side of Lut (peace be upon him), it is likewise.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 6, verse 87:

When He - glorified is He - had specified these (prophets), and concluded with the preference of each over the worlds, He followed it, in summary fashion, with the statement that others besides them were also guided, and that the excellence of these (prophets) is the cause of the specification (of guidance) for them by their names. So He said, encouraging the treading of this path by the multitude of those who travel it, and urging emulation of them in the goodness of steadfastness upon it and in conduct within it: ﴿And from﴾, meaning: and We guided, or: and We preferred, from ﴿their fathers﴾, meaning their forebears, ﴿and their descendants﴾, meaning from their offspring, men and women, ﴿and their brothers﴾, meaning the branches of their forebears. He joined to the implied verb His saying: ﴿and We chose them﴾, meaning: and We selected them.
